entries.content:
The late Nigerian sculptor Erhabor Emokpae is perhaps best known for his bronze replica of the sixteenth-century ivory mask of Queen Idia, the kingdom of Benin’s premier iyoba, or queen mother. The year was 1977. Nigeria had attained political independence from Britain less than two decades earlier and been through a bitter civil war in the late 1960s. Seeking to prove its stability and assert its influence on the continent, the young country hosted the Second World Black and African Festival of Arts and Culture (FESTAC)—at the time the largest gathering of artists from Africa and its diaspora ever convened. Emokpae’s mask, cast from a carving by the lesser-known artist Pa Joseph Alufa Obgayabona, served as the emblem of the event.

The festival’s national committee chose Queen Idia as a powerful precolonial symbol of resilience: believed by some to be the force behind the throne during her son Ésigie’s reign, she led armies to defend Benin’s sovereignty. After her death, Ésigie commissioned masks to memorialize her by Benin’s bronze and ivory casting guilds. But the selection was also a response to the British Museum’s effective denial of Nigeria’s request to borrow the original mask a year earlier. The piece had come into the museum’s custody as a spoil of war; for its return on loan, the museum asked Nigeria to pay 2 million naira ($3 million) plus insurance, the equivalent of more than $16 million today. The young country refused. Emokpae’s replica—forged to replace the stolen original—symbolized Nigeria’s defiance of their former colonizers’ demands.

Emokpae was born in Benin City, once the heartland of Benin’s empire—which at its sixteenth-century peak stretched as far east as the Niger River and almost as far west as present-day Accra in Ghana, an area roughly one fifth the size of modern Nigeria. He made the mask particularly for the people of his home region, for whom the theft of the original was part of a larger story about the colonial looting of what are known as the Benin Bronzes, a collection of several thousand masks, sculptures, and other carvings made between the thirteen and nineteenth centuries, primarily of brass but also of ivory, coral, and other materials. Britain pillaged these items from Benin’s royal palace in 1897, taking them to defray the cost of what is still remembered in the region as a humiliating massacre. The Benin monarchy has been appealing to the British government to return the artifacts since at least the 1930s, emphasizing that they are not merely treasure but expressions of a people’s history.

If the desire to reclaim the bronzes has long united many Nigerians, the effort to do so has also been a reminder of Benin’s uneasy place in the federal republic. While colonialism disrupted most regional social and political structures in West Africa, Benin’s monarchy persevered; a single family line has held onto the crown for over eight centuries and today maintains ceremonial importance and political influence, despite lacking a formal function in governance. When Nigeria gained independence in 1960, Benin retained a distinct identity.* Many of the local Bini people understood themselves to be newly subject to the Nigerian state much as they had previously been ruled by the British crown. After the British Museum refused to loan out the Queen Idia mask, Akenzua II, the oba, or king, is said to have told Nigerian government officials that “Benin’s forefathers made the first bronzes, and they’d do it again.” The comment expressed pride in his ancestors’ aptitude—but it also seemed to emphasize his kingdom’s claim to the artifact over that of the postcolonial state’s.

Nearly half a century later, these tensions have come to a head with the return of many of the bronzes. Though the British Museum has continued to deny Nigeria’s requests, other museums in the UK, US, and Europe, along with private donors, have collectively agreed to send back over a thousand items in the last decade, as global discourse on art restitution and repatriation has gathered force. “It’s a thing of joy that the objects are coming in our time,” Mark Olaitan, the curator of Nigeria’s National Museum, Benin City, told me in November. At first, many Nigerians could hardly believe that they would be the generation to see the items’ return: “People saw it as fables.”

The question of how to receive the returning bronzes fell to the Benin Dialogue Group, a coalition formed in 2007 and made up of delegates from major international museums and officials from the Nigerian government and Benin’s Royal Court. In 2020 the group’s local partner, the newly established nonprofit Legacy Restoration Trust, announced plans for a state-of-the-art museum where the objects could be conserved and made available to the public. The institution, which is now known as the Museum of West African Art (MOWAA), quickly won promises of financial support from European organizations and from the government of Edo State, of which Benin City is the capital. Phillip Ihenacho, MOWAA’s director, initially envisioned it as a place both for repatriated objects, starting with the bronzes, and for work by contemporary artists. “When we started, it was sort of a dual mission,” he told me last year. “Then we rapidly discovered how emotional and intense and far from clear a lot of the restitution discussion is.”

By the time MOWAA was set to open its doors to the public last November, a protracted struggle had rerouted the returning bronzes: they had instead ended up in the oba’s palace and Benin’s National Museum, a long-standing institution under the auspices of Nigeria’s National Commission for Museums and Monuments (NCMM). Yet that didn’t stop protesters from disrupting MOWAA’s preview opening for select guests—European and American patrons and diplomats, Nigerian literati and elite, and members of the international press, myself included—by storming the grounds and heckling attendees, accusing the institution of a lack of transparency and of bypassing traditional authorities in its quest to claim the bronzes. Almost a year later, the museum remains closed indefinitely, with viewings only by appointment. The bronzes have finally come home—but home has proved to be a fraught idea.

The tension over who should receive the bronzes first became evident in the strained relationship between Godwin Obaseki, the former governor of Edo State, and the current oba, Ewuare II. The oba asserts—and many Bini people agree—that the bronzes rightfully belong to him because most of them were commissioned by obas and crafted by the guilds in the royal court. In 2018 Obaseki’s government, at the oba’s urging, announced plans to house the bronzes in a “Benin Royal Museum” that would exist independently of the NCMM and have more advanced infrastructure for displaying the items than the Benin National Museum has; construction was to be funded by Benin Dialogue Group members like the British Museum and Germany’s Museum am Rothenbaum. But the institution never materialized, reportedly due to disputes between Obaseki and Ewuare II over funding, location, and control. While the oba continues to push for the creation of the royal museum, Obaseki soon pivoted to advocating for MOWAA’s establishment instead.

The monarchy and its supporters did not look kindly on Obaseki’s promotion of a project that competed with the oba’s own bid for donors. At a press conference in July 2021 Ewuare II denounced the governor for backing MOWAA: “The right and only legitimate destination for the artifacts to be repatriated, as already pronounced by my father, is under the aegis of the Benin Royal Museum that will be sited within the precincts of the Palace of the Oba of Benin, from where they were looted.”

The conflict between the two men arguably has its origins as far back as 1897: Obaseki is the direct descendant of Agho Obaseki, who was appointed acting prime minister of the Benin kingdom by the British after they exiled the sitting oba, Ovonramwen. In 1914, when the British merged the Southern Nigerian Protectorate (which included the Benin kingdom) and the Northern Nigerian Protectorate to form the Nigeria colony, they elevated Agho to the position of iyase—the highest-ranking chief title in the Benin kingdom. Agho’s ascension put him at odds with Oba Eweka II, who had succeeded Ovonramwen after he died in exile. Obaseki’s forefather is remembered as a shrewd, clearsighted figure who kept the kingdom from being entirely subsumed by the colony, negotiating to maintain features of the monarchy’s administration. But he is also derided, even today, as a self-serving traitor to the oba dynasty.

The oba’s part in contemporary events may surprise outsiders. Despite lacking any constitutional power, he holds influence over many facets of life in Benin’s heartland: he remains the divine leader according to the traditional religion; customarily presides over, or is at least consulted on, local affairs, including land disputes; and acts as the primary custodian of Benin’s culture and heritage. And in the case of MOWAA, he made it clear that he was discontented with a cultural institution ostensibly being built in service of that heritage. (The Benin Royal Council, which reports to the oba, did not return requests for comment; the oba himself rarely gives interviews for cultural and religious reasons.)

In addition to the oba’s disapproval, the museum had to confront the reality that Benin City is hardly the natural place for such an institution. It lacks the infrastructure of Abuja, Nigeria’s capital, or Lagos, a cultural metropolis in its own right—both of which boast a wealth of modern galleries and other arts establishments, as well as scores of affluent potential benefactors with international connections. In Benin, by contrast, despite an ongoing, rapid process of urban renewal, MOWAA is an anomaly.

The fight over the museum was encapsulated by a disagreement over its name: at first MOWAA was to be called the Edo Museum of West African Art, for the Nigerian state where it is located. “Edo” is the autochthonous name for the region’s people; they were christened the “Bini” by the Portuguese, who arrived in the kingdom in the fifteenth century and derived the name from that of the kingdom’s capital, Ubini. But it seemed that to the oba and many others, the inclusion of Edo in the proposed name both signified a blessing that hadn’t been given and represented a shift in focus toward the broader region and away from Benin City. Ihenacho confirmed that the state’s name was dropped due to “strained relationships” between Obaseki’s and Ewuare’s camps.

In March 2023 Nigeria’s outgoing president, the late Muhammadu Buhari, took the monarchy’s side in the contretemps, decreeing that the bronzes would be returned to the oba’s custody. His announcement dismayed both the NCMM, then active in the return negotiations, and some of the Western stakeholders who had backed MOWAA’s construction. One unnamed NCMM official told the BBC that Buhari’s statement was “written by someone who doesn’t understand how museums work.” The decision effectively undercut the NCMM’s ability to negotiate for the bronzes on Nigeria’s behalf. It may also hinder the agency in future international negotiations by setting a precedent that could encourage other customary rulers to assert claims over precolonial art and objects. 

One half of MOWAA’s dual mission had officially become moot. But construction continued even without the bronzes or the oba’s blessing. Foreign backers like GIZ, a German enterprise that funds sustainable development, and the Mellon Foundation were still willing to support the museum as a home for contemporary West African artists and arts education. Yet no one involved with the project seems to have entirely anticipated the confusion and suspicion that the oba’s opposition would stoke in the region. Some people didn’t understand that the museum would not, after all, host the bronzes, and resented it for claiming an inheritance that they felt belonged with the oba; others, aware of the change, questioned why the project was still going ahead and speculated about a concealed financial motive. “There’s a lot of people thinking that this is a private business where money is going to be made, that the former governor has some financial interest,” Ihenacho told me. “Some of this stuff you hear anecdotally, you don’t really believe that people think it—until you see that people do.”

I landed in Benin City for MOWAA’s opening last November to frantic messages from colleagues and public relations personnel telling me to come at once—or not at all. Instinctively, I did the former. When I arrived some of the protesters—mostly young men who couldn’t have been older than twenty-five—had reassembled after being dispersed by the city’s police a few hours earlier. Some still had sticks or stones in their hands and were wearing red hats, a nod to the coral cap worn by the oba and high-ranking chiefs in the kingdom. A handful of bored-looking police officers stood nearby. On my way to the entrance, I spoke to a group of protesters in Delta Pidgin; my own family is Urhobo and from Delta State, which borders Edo, and the languages share enough vocabulary that we were able to communicate. They let me pass without the heckling they had directed at other guests.

The protests continued after I entered the museum, and later forced many of us who were there that day to exit in small groups through a side entrance. They spurred MOWAA to cancel the rest of the events planned for the preview, including a historical site tour, campus talks, and a day-long symposium on African art. The vast majority of the protesters were poor or working class; many were disaffected youth, and some were members of local social and cultural groups loosely affiliated with the Palace. None would speak to me on the record, but they made their dissatisfaction known on Nigerian television news and social media, decrying what they considered the museum’s lack of clarity about its purpose and its failure to respect the oba’s authority. They insinuated that MOWAA was profiting from their history and their land without their consent. Edobor Osazee, Coordinator of the Coalition of Benin Socio-Cultural Organisations (CBSCO), told Nigeria’s Television Continental News that the process by which the museum was established was “cunning and crafty.” In the same segment another unidentified protester said of MOWAA, “They know what they are doing. They want to catch us unaware and that is why they came on Sunday because most of us went to church. But thank God and our ancestors who was able to awaken us and say we should go and stop them.”

Nevertheless, the preview’s attendees appeared absorbed. I was captivated by the modern, rammed-earth exterior of the building, which was designed by the renowned Ghanaian-British architect David Adjaye. (He received the commission before he was accused of sexual misconduct by three of his former employees in 2023.) Inside, the 48,000-square-foot museum was full of gleaming galleries and boasted a 180-seat auditorium and a state-of-the art lab devoted to material science, archaeological research, and art restoration. Archaeologists affiliated with the museum had already begun extensive excavations of Edo artifacts in the city and started conducting scientific analyses on objects from across West Africa.

The exhibition on display in the atrium was a limited survey of West African history as told through objects and sculptures representing different nations and ethnic groups. The majority were of Yoruba origin, reflecting the group’s cultural dominance and ethnic privilege—and, arguably, the Yoruba’s longstanding tradition of cultural exchange. I paused in front of the copper mask of Obalufon, the third ooni, or traditional ruler, of Ilé-Ifẹ̀, the ancient city and spiritual home of the Yoruba people, located in what is now Osun State. The early fourteenth-century mask, which has hollow, almond-shaped eyes and small, round punctures around the mouth and chin—“possibly designed for attaching a ceremonial beard,” as the description noted—was on loan from the National Museum’s Lagos division. There wasn’t much to be found of the Binis here. I wondered if this would make the protesters outside, and MOWAA’s local detractors in general, more or less displeased.

When I spoke with MOWAA’s modern and contemporary curator, Aindrea Emelife, the following day, she defended the museum’s collection. “Whilst there wasn’t such presence of Benin objects, there was presence of Benin history,” she said. She pointed to the inclusion of a piece by the artist Isaac Emokpae that engages with the work of his late father, the famed Erhabor. She also noted that while about 70 percent of the works on display are Nigerian, the museum has also tried to represent other countries in West Africa “because quite frankly—and I can say this because I’m Nigerian—we do take up the conversation.”

The preview’s main attraction was “Nigeria Imaginary: Homecoming,” an exhibition of work by eleven artists, seven of whom were shown in Nigeria’s pavilion at the 2024 Venice Biennale. That show was criticized for featuring only one artist who lives and works primarily in Nigeria—a problem Emelife sought to rectify by adding four more. MOWAA described the art on view as focusing on “questions of nationhood,” though they defined the word broadly. Toyin Ojih Odutola’s Lęhin Mgbede (Before +After the Evening’s Performance) (2023–2024), for example, a diptych using layered pastel, charcoal, and graphite on linen, depicts a cast of characters preceding and following some unseen event. It is a testament to Odutola’s personal experience of mourning her grandmother that at the same time conveys a transethnic Nigerian sensibility: our ancestors, it emphasizes, remain constant guides even as we transition between life and death. Yinka Shonibare’s Monument to the Restitution of the Mind and Soul (2024), meanwhile, consists of 153 clay replicas of the stolen Benin treasures along with a Batik-patterned bust of Sir Harry Rawson, the British naval officer who led the 1897 attack.

One of the Nigeria-based artists added to the show was Isaac Emokpae (he splits his time between Lagos and Reading, England). Walking through the galleries, I spotted him looking delighted, taking a picture of his mixed-media painting Sarkin Amina (The Story of a Monarch) (2025). It’s a reinterpretation of the story of Queen Amina, the sixteenth-century leader of the precolonial Hausa Kingdom of Zazzau, now in the northern Nigerian state of Zaria. As the first woman to rule Zazzau—remaining unmarried while doing so—she commanded formidable military campaigns that expanded her kingdom’s size and riches. Emokpae explained that he was drawn to Queen Amina because, like Queen Idia, she defied the constraints placed on women and left a legacy in the place she ruled. From the city walls she constructed to the trade routes she forged, “Amina is very influential in how northern Nigeria became the way we know it today.”

Sarkin Amina also references a 1976 oil painting of the same subject, Queen Amina of Zaria, by Emokpae’s father. The older Emokpae shows Queen Amina twice: on one side of the canvas, she rides on horseback with sword in hand, leading her soldiers into battle; her portrait gazes out from the other side, in a muted red dress and orange head covering, with a phlegmatic disposition. In the younger Emokpae’s interpretation she wears the colors of royalty, a long blue dress and velvet head covering of deep violet. At her feet appear to be her subjects, while just behind her are guards in red tagelmust and litham—the cloth mouth-veils and turbans traditionally worn by men in parts of the Sahara region. In a scene visible over her shoulder, a girl—Amina as a child—play-fights with a boy, using sticks as swords. When he spoke to me in January from his studio in Reading, Emokpae told me that a detail in that background, a praying mantis on a clay sill behind the queen’s guards, represents her sexual independence. (The insect “eats a male counterpart after mating,” he pointed out.)

Later it occurred to me that Queen Amina could also be understood as a symbol of Nigerian national unity, a way to declare that the history of northern Nigeria belongs, in a sense, to all of us. In “Nigeria Imaginary: Homecoming,” first conceived for an international audience, I saw MOWAA’s aspiration to serve as a home for contemporary global art—but also its ambition to take part in remaking Nigerian nationhood amid imperial histories that assembled diverse groups into a single polity. This very objective honors the history of the Bini, whose kingdom, empire that it was, always comprised a multitude of different peoples.

But even if MOWAA is very much for Nigeria and Nigerians, is it really for the Bini? It was notable that the preview was timed to follow on the heels of Lagos’s tenth international art fair, ART x Lagos. Many guests, myself included, attended the larger event before traveling to the MOWAA opening, only an hour’s flight away. Press previews, of course, are never intended for the public; still, save for the volunteers, this one was almost entirely a gathering of outsiders—a detail easily misconstrued by residents. Some locals clearly took from our presence that MOWAA may be in their home, but it is not their museum.

Ihenacho told me that he regrets not communicating the museum’s mission more clearly. “Maybe we should try to speak more loudly about what we are but also what we are not,” he told me. “Much misperception still exists about who we are, about how we originated, about who has an interest.” Perhaps MOWAA could have taken greater care to reach locals in forums they frequent—including on WhatsApp, where all Nigerian news and gossip lives many lifetimes. They could also have brought more local artists into the museum’s orbit. When I spoke to young artists in Benin City, many seemed to feel that, as the budding contemporary painter Derek Jahyém Jombo-Ogboi put it, residents “didn’t have a say.”

Certainly, the MOWAA preview made a sharp contrast with a truly local arts event that began on the same day: the Black Muse Arts Festival, put on by the internationally acclaimed, Edo State–born artist and writer Victor Ehikhamenor. The festival took place in a park in Benin City’s residential Iyekogba neighborhood. Entry was free; attendees drifted through the open, convivial gathering and ate “small chops,” jollof, and sweets from local businesses. A young multidisciplinary artist from Benin City, Osaru Obaseki (no direct relation to the governor), won first prize for Coat of Many Lines, a pair of casted bronze busts. People remarked on how the event had beautified the neighborhood, bringing not only the sculptural installations—which remained until April of this year—but also a forty-nine-foot vaulted pavilion made from bamboo, the work of the Nigerian architect James Inedu-George.

MOWAA’s future, meanwhile, remains uncertain. According to Nigerian news networks, Ewuare II visited the governor of Edo state, Monday Okpebholo, two days before the disastrous preview and implored him to order a full investigation into MOWAA’s finances. Okpebholo reemphasized his commitment to creating a Benin Royal Museum. “The issue of MOWAA is over,” he told the oba and the rest of the audience. “It was a gift to Your Majesty, and it will be restored as such”—which is to say, converted into the royal museum that Obaseki’s government had first imagined back in 2018. (The royal palace hasn’t released any formal statement on MOWAA in the months since.)

The day after the preview, Okpebholo reportedly revoked the museum’s Certificate of Occupancy, nullifying its right to use the land on which it sits. The Nigerian press suggested that the governor wanted to restore the land to its previous purpose as the site of the Benin Central Hospital, although that explanation seems unconvincing: the hospital’s services were relocated after its facilities were deemed inadequate in 2021. So far the museum remains in place, neither open to the public nor shut down by the state. It is an institution in abeyance. 

Still, the debacle does not seem beyond solving. In late November, President Bola Tinubu set up a committee to bring together representatives of the oba, leading officials from the cultural sector (including Hannatu Musawa, Nigeria’s Minister of Art, Culture, Tourism, and the Creative Economy), and French and German emissaries. The group has been tasked with submitting a “comprehensive framework for the permanent resolution” of the dispute directly to the president, though is has not been given a deadline, and the art ministry did not respond to multiple requests for comment. One might hope that Nigerians, who were once a people loath to broadcast embarrassments on this scale, would be determined—even after years of incompetent governance—to save face by any possible means.

To succeed, MOWAA will need the oba’s support, or at least his acquiescence, which would encourage the city’s inhabitants to view the institution in a new light. In November, on the day it announced its indefinite closure—the day before it was supposed to open to the public—MOWAA posted a detailed statement to its website aiming to “clarify recent misconceptions circulating about its mission, holdings, and role,” emphasizing that they held the oba in “the highest esteem,” and stressing that the museum “does not hold, nor have we ever claimed title” to the bronzes. In February Ihenacho personally released another statement proposing listening sessions to be held across Nigeria and West Africa from March to May, to help the museum “consider how cultural institutions can be grounded, responsive, and accountable to their publics.” 

Benin history is full of disputes between obas and chiefs, often with much more at stake than a contemporary art museum. The oba dynasty has survived precisely because it knows how to adapt to its surroundings while maintaining its authority. MOWAA, if its most influential stakeholders have a sense of humor, might even create an exhibit to honor this feature of Bini history; it could nod to ancient Benin’s guilds by commissioning works from artists in the city. Such an exhibition could perhaps include contemporary brass masks and figurines that would tell the story of the obas. That way, MOWAA could end up displaying some Benin Bronzes after all.

The historic bronzes, meanwhile, have been arriving in waves since 2022, to the unbridled joy of Benin City residents. The local press documented the oba dancing when wooden and bronze stools arrived from Germany in 2024; according to Olaitan, people throughout the city were equally jubilant. Over one hundred artifacts, mainly from the Netherlands, were already on display at Benin’s National Museum as of last November. Hundreds more will return this year from England and elsewhere, all legally owned by the oba.

When I visited the National Museum during my trip to Benin City, the brilliance of the returned bronzes was slightly dimmed by their surroundings. The placards describing the items were terse and printed on flimsy-looking white cardboard. I wondered how much care had been taken in the placement of each item; the masks tell a story, but their display did not. The facilities paled beside those I’d just seen at MOWAA. I felt that the Benin Royal Museum could not come to fruition soon enough.

And yet among the many marvelous objects—meticulously articulated plaques of obas and warrior chiefs in ceremonial regalia, ritual and fighting swords, life-like cockerels and crocodiles, and more—was an ivory mask of Queen Idia, repatriated in 2022. The British Museum still holds one likeness; this one was repatriated by the Linden Museum in Stuttgart, Germany, though the placard incorrectly stated that it had been returned by the Smithsonian. The top of this Idia’s forehead is wrapped in coral beads, separating the decorative pattern of her headdress from the incision lines just above her eyes, marks she is said to have obtained around the time of her marriage to Oba Ozolua, Oba Ésigie’s father, and which supposedly furnished her with arcane powers. She wears the stern and watchful expression of a matriarch. I was happy to see her there, in her home.

entries.content:
This article is part of a regular series of conversations with the Review’s contributors; read past entries here and sign up for our email newsletter to get them delivered to your inbox each week.

Writing for the NYR Online from India’s Cockroach Janata Party protests this summer, Poorna Swami explained the young protesters’ outrage at the corruption and authoritarianism of the Modi government, offered a concise history of antigovernment agitation in India, and laid out the complicated social forces that brought these students together in the street across lines of caste, religion, and gender. Swami is herself a student, working on a Ph.D. at Harvard’s Department of South Asian Studies, as well as a translator of Urdu, a dancer, and a longtime cultural critic. On the streets of Delhi, among protesters marching under the constant threat of violence, she saw the movement’s leaders attempt to subdue political chants; Hindu-nationalist sympathizers chanting along with anticaste activists; and the daring jocularity of the young people assembled before baton-wielding policemen, especially evident in their famous “sexualized posters: ‘Daddy, beat me.’”

Swami’s earlier essays for the NYR Online have brought her historical and political analysis to bear on cultural matters; as she told me, “I’m interested in how the past pushes against the present.” Her essay about the great qawwali musician Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan includes a thrilling and immersive description of the atmosphere around his appearance at a music festival in 1985, years before she was born—but Swami has been an acolyte in the cult of Nusrat her whole life; her father had even made a short film about him, “a love letter to Nusrat.”

We emailed last week about matters personal and political: her artistic childhood in Bangalore, her experience on the streets of Delhi, and her hopes about what this summer’s uprising means for the future of India.

Nawal Arjini: How did you come to have an interest in the arts, and especially the performing arts? When did your interests in music (particularly Nusrat) and film emerge, and how were they nurtured—were there any particular institutions, works of art, or artists that encouraged deeper examination?

Poorna Swami: It was an unusual childhood: my parents were both painters, my grandparents worked in independent cinema, and most of my family was in some way involved with theater. At first I just napped backstage, then I dabbled as a stagehand, then I designed costumes, then acted. Anything we did as a family involved the arts somehow. My father took me to art galleries, with my grandfather I watched way too many age-inappropriate films, my grandmother took me to bookstores and music stores. She and I would use two separate bookmarks in the same book if we were reading it together but at different paces. I painted and danced and was an annoying kid who, at thirteen, decided to make a camcorder documentary about music in Bangalore. There was a brief period when I’d convinced myself that I’d study sociology in college, but I ended up pretty close to the family trade.

I grew up in a house that wasn’t really religious, which wasn’t all that common in 1990s India. So any sense I had of Hinduism and Islam—the two religious traditions that ran in my family—was through music, literature, and paintings around the house. Nusrat was also the soundtrack to my parents’ short-lived marriage and, as I mentioned in the essay, he was a part of my earliest memories. As a child I found a lot of his songs very danceable, but as I grew older, my mother and grandmother began to explain the lyrics and the spiritual message behind them. By the time I was a teenager, we were looking up words from his songs in dictionaries to find additional meanings. Now that I think of it, that exercise probably led me to literary translation later in life.

You have written in the past about the difficulties in researching a play, for instance, many years after it was performed. As a researcher and a critic of historical performances—theater, dance, music—how do you deal with such ephemeral material?

When the past becomes harder to trace it’s a fun challenge for me. I am a real archive nut, so going on wild-goose chases is something I enjoy; I looked for that play—a 1963 production of The Flaming Spear/No Other Way, an Indian play about the Mau Mau rebellion—for maybe a year, writing to people and going through the dusty, unorganized cupboards of a theater troupe in Mumbai. This slightly insane approach doesn’t always work out, as it didn’t in that case. So I had to recreate the play from a handful of photographs and short newspaper reviews of performances from the 1960s.

Again, archives helped me find my way into a text and a moment in time that I couldn’t know firsthand. But of course, archives don’t tell you everything. Any good historian will tell you that archives also exclude groups and distort the past. But piecing small things together to build a story excites me. I find disproportionate pleasure in laboring over tiny details, like the weather in a given city on a certain day forty years ago or the gestures of a now dead poet. It’s not just big, fancy libraries but often people’s under-the-bed junk that has given me interesting nuggets to write about. Finding my father’s film on Nusrat is a good example.

Advertisement

You are also a translator, and so you must deal with another kind of intangibility. Do you have a philosophy when it comes to literary translation?

I’m still figuring it out. Sometimes I find I have to let go, to keep some meanings in translation and relinquish others. After all, a text has multiple meanings even in the original, and not every native reader gets all of them. But sometimes I might sneak in a gloss, or attempt some kind of sleight of hand to introduce context. When translating modern poetry I have a lot of affinity for sound and texture. I try to strike a balance between conveying the meanings of individual words and phrases and retaining a sense of what I felt about the poem’s grain as I was reading the original. There are these opening lines from a Jack Gilbert poem that I often come back to: “How astonishing it is that language can almost mean,/and frightening that it does not quite.” Language is at once capacious and imprecise, and while translating, I try to remind myself of that, lest I fall into an endless cycle of handwringing.

Would you tell us a bit about the writer you’re translating at the moment, Fahmida Riaz?

Fahmida Riaz was an incredible Urdu poet from Pakistan, arguably the most prominent female Urdu poet of the twentieth century. She was a Marxist and a feminist, and in the 1970s and early 1980s she ran this dissident magazine called Awaz, which published pro-democracy op-eds and translations of African and Asian literature in Urdu. During Zia-ul-Haq’s military dictatorship, the magazine was banned and Riaz faced multiple charges of sedition, which could have led to capital punishment. So she fled across the border to India and spent seven years in exile there. It’s amazing, given India and Pakistan’s adverse political relations, that Riaz was given asylum by the Indian state—in fact, by the prime minister personally.

Although Riaz is perhaps Urdu’s quintessential feminist poet—what Forugh Farrokhzad is for Farsi—her exile years tend to be mentioned only in passing. I’ve been researching that period of her life and translating her exile poems into English for the first time. I’ve scoured libraries in both India and Pakistan, begged her friends and family to let me ransack their personal collections for letters and photographs, and spent hours talking to people on both sides of the border to put together an account of how she spent her exile years and what the fallout was once she returned. It’s a project that brings together literature, political history, and feminism. The translation is called Guilty as Charged: poems of exile and will be out in 2027 from Ugly Duckling Presse in the US and Poetry Translation Center in the UK.

That takes us to India: How was the first news of the protests received among your friends and family?

To be honest, most of them didn’t take the Cockroach Janata Party too seriously at first. Online, we saw people wearing cockroach costumes and doing sporadic demonstrations in different parts of India, but those seemed to be social media larks. When a more formal sit-in started in June, again, it seemed a bit scattered and, at that point, sorely lacking in concrete aims. And then when Sonam Wangchuck joined the protest, becoming a sort of figurehead, people in my circle were wary.

In 2011, when the Congress Party was in power, there were huge anticorruption protests in Delhi led by a self-described Gandhian activist named Anna Hazare, a man who went on a hunger strike. The origins of that popular movement were murky, and later many people alleged that it had been orchestrated by the BJP and its right-wing parent organization, the RSS. Certainly that 2011 movement helped take down the ruling government and usher in the era of Modi. Given this history, many people around me were skeptical of the provenance of a group like the CJP, especially because some of its leaders had, in the past, been affiliated with the Aam Aadmi Party (another political party that emerged from the 2011 protests). Many wondered if it was only a matter of time before some established political party came in and took over this new movement, too. It didn’t help that leading the demonstration in Delhi was another fasting, middle-aged man—one who was known to have collaborated with the BJP in the past.

Advertisement

But when the left-wing student organizations began to have a more prominent position in the protests—sharpening the messages that went out from the street, bringing actual college students to the ground, and going on hunger strike themselves—there was clearer anti-BJP sentiment and more organized agitation. When the police kidnapped Wangchuk, it actually helped stir up momentum. I showed up in person because I knew something was changing. By the time extensive police violence broke out on July 20, the movement had spread far beyond the grip of the CJP and Wangchuk and that helped counter some of the early reservations that people around me had.

Did you ever imagine that such a substantial protest movement would arise among students, or among young people more broadly?

Not really. Earlier waves of student protests had been met with such immense repression, and some of those leaders are still behind bars without trial. University campuses have also become so heavily policed in the last decade that I didn’t think there was any room for an uprising. The willingness of students (especially those from majority religious and caste backgrounds) to directly take on the state at its most violent was not something I expected.

Is a sense of generational warfare as pervasive in India as it is here?

I don’t think so. Respecting one’s elders is encoded into Indian life in a very different way—deference is a given. But that’s why these protests have been so remarkable. We’re seeing such a clear and vocal generational break for the first time. I met students who had showed up to protest without telling their parents. Children of BJP leaders were also reported to have turned up. The leader of the All-India Students’ Association, Neha Bora, said she went on hunger strike without her BJP-supporting parents knowing. The unfiltered language and near-bacchanalian texture of these protests was not something we’d seen before. Gen Z, who had been written off as lacking both purpose and politics, suddenly asserted themselves with reels and memes, eventually taking direct aim at the prime minister. Part of the success (and fun) of these recent protests was watching older media commentators and authorities try to decipher the various viral trends the young protesters unleashed.

To what extent do you think the protests, and the spirit with which they were received by the nonprotesting part of India, have shifted the terrain of political life?

It’s hard to say, especially because there haven’t been any elections yet. One also has to remember that many of the young protesters have never voted. I did ask a bunch of young people if they’d sign up and actually vote in the next election. Most of them said yes, but not all of them committed to writing off the BJP for good. Because a large segment of protesters claimed a kind of “nonideological” stance, they garnered a lot of sympathy from people outside the movement, who saw students as the “future of the country” asking for nothing more than “their basic rights.”

But now that the movement has gone beyond a headline-grabbing, site-specific demonstration, and even the CJP is much more vocal about its indictment of the BJP, I am curious to see what, if any, kind of electoral shift we will see down the line. There’s been renewed momentum two months later: the CJP is now calling for the resignation of the chief of the Election Commission of India, whom they allege has rigged the country’s electoral rolls in favor of the BJP. Left-wing student organizations are leading a parallel campaign on the same issue. It’s also not just about youth and student groups. The Congress, the main opposition party in India, and its leader, Rahul Gandhi, have been campaigning hard on student issues and have pushed the government on its brutal response to the July protests, though their agenda continues to remain separate from that of the CJP and the left. It would be a gross overstatement to claim that this scenario is the end of Modi and the BJP. Hindu nationalism’s takeover of India’s public institutions and its social fabric runs too deep. But at the same time, the country has not seen such a large movement in six years, and certainly not with such broad appeal.

How has your sense of the protests changed since they began, and since they ended?

I am definitely a lot less cynical. Even though I questioned many aspects of the protests, being there in person made me realize that in whatever imperfect way, an unlikely range of people were coming together to show their dissatisfaction—and that in itself was unprecedented.

I am not holding my breath to see if the CJP makes electoral strides. I think the significance of these protests has been that they enabled all kinds of young people to voice their opinions about the only government they have ever known. We’re also seeing a new generation of student leaders come up (campus politics in India are more directly connected with national politics than in the US): Neha Bora has emerged as a tremendous force, perhaps the most clear-sighted leader throughout this movement. And most importantly, the BJP’s inability to keep up with the language of a generation that is master of the Internet has been entirely exposed. Try as they might, there’s no way the government can erase how, at the height of the protests, young people had reduced Modi to a joke. If they did that once, and with such panache, I think they could do it again.
