entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
I met Karan Mahajan, the Indian-American novelist and essayist, in 2018, when we were both fellows at the Cullman Center of the New York Public Library. Karan was beginning to write The Complex, his novel that has just been released; I was finishing The Enigma of Clarence Thomas. I was drawn to Karan right away. Not only is he one of the best talkers in the world, ready to go anywhere in a conversation, but he’s also genuinely interested in right-wing politics. Since the rise of Trump, many on the left have tried to gain a better understanding of the right. Karan’s aims are both more modest and more ambitious. He wants to think and feel with the right. The Complex is one of those surprisingly rare novels that engages with the inner life of far-right leaders in the mold of India’s Modi, and of the ordinary people who vote for them. In this conversation, Karan and I talked about how the novel tells the story of the last seventy-five years of Indian politics, as well as the challenges of inhabiting the minds of right-wing characters. —Corey Robin

Corey Robin: Why did you choose The Complex as the title? What does it refer to?

Karan Mahajan: On the most basic level, the title refers to the complex in Delhi in which the large extended family at the heart of the novel lives. More importantly, the title reflects the mindsets of the characters in the book. Laxman Chopra, who is one of the main players, is the youngest of nine and a loser who’s trying to measure himself up against his late “great father.” He has a complex vis-à-vis his relatives who have immigrated to the US, even though those people don’t find their lives particularly satisfying, and he’s complexed in relation to this pantheon of independence-era figures—his father being one of them—who seem to have achieved epochal greatness. Laxman doesn’t see a means of achieving that in 1980s India, at the grubby end of the mixed economy, of the socialist dream of Nehru.

At another point in the novel, there’s a more capitalist character, Sachin, who says to his wife, “The whole country is complexed thanks to Nehru’s socialist policies.” His wife disagrees.

Robin: Tell me more about SP Chopra, who’s the founder of this family and the complex, but who’s also a founder of modern India. That theme—that founders of families are also founders of countries—is such a rich subject in my field, political theory, and yours, literature. Could you talk about the tensions and parallels between the founding of the family and the founding of India?

Mahajan: I wanted to pick a very particular kind of individual as the figurehead of this novel. SP Chopra is a freedom fighter, but he’s also a banker who’s extending loans to Indian revolutionaries and to the British. He is libertarian in his impulses. He’s not aligned with Nehru. He belongs to this whole strand of Indian history that’s been forgotten, one which included the pro-business Swatantra Party. SP’s attitudes are then amplified by Laxman, who seeks an ideology but lacks his father’s substance.

I wouldn’t necessarily call it a negative inheritance. But an inheritance can be completely warped, much as we see with “Make America Great Again.”

Nor did I want SP Chopra to be revealed to be a fraud. Maybe there can be goodness and greatness in one’s past, even if it’s not the kind that I completely agree with. But does this past have to be a liability, especially in the male psyche? Why can’t one escape or process an inheritance and forge ahead? Why are societies at large panicking when they look around at the newer, hybrid world we all inhabit—one in which women are security guards and Dalits are behind the desks of government offices—and thinking: We need to go back?

These questions came out organically in writing the novel, and especially when Laxman, who is really detestable, becomes a negative narrative engine. He possesses the energy in the novel, in much the same way that right-wing movements command political energy right now.

Robin: The parallels between Laxman and Trump are clear. He’s corrupt, he’s skimming off the temple’s coffers to fund his business, and he’s also a failed businessman. His father thinks he’s an idiot. Even he thinks he’s an idiot. He’s filled with humiliation and resentment. He’s a sexual predator. Yet Laxman is a surprisingly sympathetic character. He has genuine love for one of the women he ends up having an affair with. He’s self-aware: he sees himself as other people see him, and he’s forward and direct. I’m interested in the novel’s sympathy toward him. I’m also interested in a claim repeated by many characters in the novel: that Laxman is born to be a political person. What is it about him that makes him seem so eligible for political life?

Advertisement

Mahajan: This is where maybe Trump was in the back of my mind. The other characters notice his shamelessness, his ability to move forward and not be stymied by conscience.

Robin: But he has something that Trump doesn’t have: self-consciousness, self-awareness. Shameless people usually don’t see themselves as other people see them.

Mahajan: True, but he has a blind spot. He’s not concerned with how people who are less powerful than him will perceive him. For example, he thinks, I can take liberties with this woman. She will probably not like me, but it doesn’t matter. Yet he doesn’t want shame to be brought upon his nuclear unit or the extended family. He wants to be perceived as respecting the hierarchy of the clan.

After I was done with the book, I remember thinking about something you wrote in The Reactionary Mind: about how conservatives see democratic movements as “a terrible disturbance in the private life of power,” and how the conservative or reactionary response has been to “cede the field of the public, if you must, but stand fast in the private.” Laxman acts out in the private sphere in response to public disappointment.

For me, as a writer, the key moment in the novel occurs when Laxman’s opportunism gives way to ideology. It’s the year 1984. The nascent BJP has been decimated at the polls following the anti-Sikh riots and Indira Gandhi’s assassination. Yet Laxman refuses to give up on the BJP. He has fully absorbed a doctrine of resenting minorities, and believes his family has been suppressed in much the same way the nation has been.

Robin: You’ve just identified part of the political appeal of these shameless figures, which is that they’re not just domineering. You show the side of them that is desperate. They start off powerless. They’re contending for power, which makes them multidimensional.

Mahajan: Laxman is also unfortunately in sync with the larger reactionary culture. In that stratum of Indian society, at that moment in history, most people would have believed that, in sexual assault, the woman is at fault. Many Punjabi Hindus would have quietly felt that Muslims and minorities were being given too many sops. Laxman’s verbalizing the impulses of the silent majority under the Congress (the secular, liberal party that dominated Indian politics for the first forty years after independence).

Robin: Your portrayal of the silent majority’s sensibility toward the Congress is subtle. The disillusionment comes out casually, in everyday conversation and throwaway references. The Congress is still a force in that it’s an institutional power, but it’s running on fumes, it’s seen as corrupt—and that’s among the Chopras, who are a family of Congress people. It reminds me of the best histories of the fall of the New Deal order, which show how there was a rot within that made it vulnerable. The question isn’t Why did it collapse? It’s Why did it take so long to collapse?

Mahajan: That’s why Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi were important to include peripherally in the novel. The Congress represents dynastic politics, and the novel unfolds in the shadow of the Emergency (the imposition of authoritarian rule by Indira Gandhi from 1975 to 1977), which partially delegitimized the Congress’s claims to being democratic. Then there are the proto-BJP people who were jailed by Indira and who, in a sense, learned the art of political repression from her. Similarly, the Congress perpetrates the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, and the BJP pretends to oppose them, only to perhaps use those riots as a model for the anti-Muslim pogrom in Gujarat in 2002 under then-chief-minister Narendra Modi.

I was interested in that iterative version of history, where you’re always learning from the thing you oppose. And I’m reminded of what you write about in The Reactionary Mind, which is that right-wing movements, for all their reactionary impulses, are often modern in attitude because they’re actively gaining energy from opposing the left. This is not a classical conservatism descending from the Vedas in India or from the Constitution in the US. I didn’t want to make Laxman a learned religious person. The culture, in fact, is sitting lightly on him, and he feels much closer to that culture when he’s opposing the regime that he thinks has been imposed on him. Or as you write, the reactionary “seeks to enjoy [his advantages] precisely as they are being—or have been—taken away.”

Advertisement

Now, I have a question for you. You’ve written two books analyzing and thinking about conservatives: The Reactionary Mind and The Enigma of Clarence Thomas. People have asked me what it feels like to “spend time” with people like Laxman whose behaviors or opinions one abhors. What is it like for you as a writer and theorist?

Robin: Until recently it wasn’t a problem. I enjoyed living with, being with, studying people who initially seemed distant and strange, even abhorrent. They felt like people who had to be figured out. Everybody has a story, which can turn into a shtick. The trick is to get inside it. And it felt like a challenge to translate what I’d found back to people who are not on the right. As with all travel writing, I had to bring these “foreign” elements back home.

But something has changed for me since the rise of Trump. I find it almost impossible to understand the anti-immigrant and xenophobic elements of the right. I don’t have an ounce of nationalism or patriotism, but the one element of American history that stirs me emotionally—the one thing that I think the United States, for all its faults, once got right—is immigration. Seeing how immigrants are always reinventing and retelling the American story, making it more alive and more present, I genuinely don’t understand how can people be against that.

A bigger challenge for me is that the right today is mostly derivative and unimaginative. When I read the right, I don’t see or hear much, at the deepest levels, that I haven’t seen or heard before. And I see a lot of scholars and journalists with a bottomless appetite for that derivativeness, and I can’t work myself up to the enthusiasms of their reading. Part of what I was drawn to in your novel is that even if the political landscape is familiar, the psychic landscape is not. It’s filled with new minds and surprises, and things blowing up in unexpected ways.

Mahajan: I wonder, though, when I hear you talk about a block, whether the xenophobic right is a subject you will end up writing about precisely because you find it hard to comprehend.

Robin: That may be a bridge too far for me.

Mahajan: What was the entry point for you into the mind of Clarence Thomas in The Enigma of Clarence Thomas?

Robin: Thomas has a story that’s rooted in the experience of the Ivy League, which is a story of humiliation and of resentment that’s familiar to me, even though he tells it through the paradigm of race and thinks that’s the only paradigm in which it can be understood. When people on the left, particularly white people, “otherize” Thomas by saying,“His whole politics of resentment is just about being snubbed at Yale,” I think, “Can’t you identify with that at all?” On the other hand, Thomas is this total narcissist who really does seem to think humiliation never happened to anyone but him.

Mahajan: In writing about figures like Thomas or Laxman, there is an automatic tension that comes into play because they have already been identified as “bad” by those most likely to read your work. Do you think that generates a frisson?

Robin: Yes, but maybe not in the way you’re getting at. There are moments in the writing where I’m inhabiting the mind of, let’s say, Thomas, and reconstructing his arguments, and I suddenly feel lift-off from the immediate evidence that’s in front of me. It feels like flying. I don’t think it’s a moral frisson, an excitement that I’m with the bad boy or something like that. It’s more like: This is somebody who is illegible to many people, and I’m rendering that person intelligible but without that simple script. To me that feels like writing.

Based on the way you deal with Laxman, I think we both know that monsters aren’t interesting if you render them as monsters.

Mahajan: I want to come back to what you said about travel. For example, I’ve noticed that, in my fiction writing, I’m not interested directly in the facts of my own life. Instead, I’m drawn to certain subjects or images in an inexplicable way. Writing about individuals with different ideologies is a version of that. I wonder if you feel less excited writing about people who are in the same ideological realm as you are because you already agree with and understand them.

Robin: Definitely. I feel that most when I’m teaching. My teaching is best when I’m dealing with writers who are not like me. The ones who are like me, I have a hard time making them interesting and worth reading. And I think that’s partly why, for many years, I stayed away from writing about the left. It’s not that I don’t think about myself and the ideas I share with the left. It’s that whenever I try to render them on the page, they feel inert.

Mahajan: Now I want to pose a moral question. Obviously, what one doesn’t want to do, as a writer, is revel in the evil or badness of a character or the worst instincts of the right. This is a point Coetzee makes in “The Problem of Evil” in Elizabeth Costello. As a novelist, my own strategy has been to inhabit my “bad” characters very physically and to let their objectionable behaviors emerge sideways, through their actions. A character’s racism, for example, wouldn’t be the center of the frame, because making it central is what the person who is viewing them as a racist is doing. But when you say that you want to “see the world through [Thomas’s] eyes,” how do you avoid the problem of, say, overly sympathizing with his views?

Robin: As you were talking, I thought of Hannah Arendt, in her portrait of Eichmann. This is exactly what she does and always gets attacked for. She writes, for example, about how, at the end of the war, when all the Nazis are trying to figure out what’s going to happen to them, Eichmann’s obsessed about whether Kaltenbrunner, who’s his senior, is going to invite him to lunch. Yet he has no memory of all these details of a transport in which tens of thousands of people were killed. People thought that Arendt was trying to diminish Eichmann’s evil, but I think she was trying to do what you’re describing: to find a way into the being of somebody who could perpetrate such crimes.

With Thomas, it wasn’t so hard, because he does it for you. In his memoir, he begins with the food that he ate in Pinpoint, this particular kind of crab and different kinds of seafood. He tells you the music he was listening to at critical moments in his life, what he was wearing. From those details and others, you begin to get a picture of someone who is definitively placed somewhere in time, who has specific tastes and preferences, distinctive dispositions, in the way all people do, that don’t tell you about his politics but do give you a feeling for him as a person. From there you start thinking about how such a person, in this case, Thomas, moves through the world as a Black man, yet says and does things that make life terrible for Black people.

Going back to Elizabeth Costello, I want to emphasize what you said, about not reveling in the evil. This is a huge problem. It’s not just an aesthetic problem; it’s a political problem. It’s one of the things that I’ve always hated about left-wing writing about the right, which is that it seems to revel in the right’s evil. But it’s a bigger challenge now. We have this cesspool in the White House, and I see the way people on the left love to talk about it. Every horrible detail. It’s a dead end—it’s like enjoying a horror movie; it’s not really thinking about what’s going on there. The alternative isn’t letting it go, maintaining silence about it, but taking those details as signs of something other than movie-level monstrosity, using them as a beginning for understanding something we didn’t understand before.

Mahajan: What are the other common mistakes that novelists and theorists make when writing about reactionaries?

Robin: There are two, and both speak to how well you write about the right. Judith Shklar, the political theorist at Harvard, wrote a book called Ordinary Vices. Her second chapter is about hypocrisy and why we hate it. But she takes great pains to remind us that hypocrisy is not the worst vice. I never appreciated her point until recently, but it’s useful advice for thinking about the right. The right’s hypocrisy often gives the left orgasms. The left always needs to relearn the lessons of Hegel and Marx—beneath any surface contradiction, there’s a complex and elusive unity. It’s our job to find it, not to dwell on the contradiction or hypocrisy, because dwelling on it keeps the unity in obscurity.

The other mistake involves how we deal with sex and shame. There’s an easy story to tell about the right’s sexual morality, which is that it derives from repressed “deviance,” that is from repressing desires that the right deems deviant yet members of the right still feel, only more so. It’s a convenient script that tells you little. Most people, across the spectrum, have all kinds of shame associated with sex. It’s part of what sex is, it’s part of what often creates desire. One of the virtues of your novel is how intelligently it deals with the subjects of sex and shame.

Mahajan: For me, my novels don’t work till I have the characters’ sexual drives figured out. I experienced this with my characters in The Association of Small Bombs as well. At the time, the larger discourse around Islamic fundamentalism was so puerile that it made my task easier in some ways. The idea that fundamentalists were committing terrorist attacks because they didn’t have sex! It’s shocking that this was a mainstream view.

But that brings me to the next question, which was the one about novels. You’ve written, “Politicians and parties talk of constitution and amendment, natural rights and inherited privileges. But the real subject of their deliberations is the private life of power…. It is also why it has so often fallen to our novelists to explain to us our politics.” Were there specific novelists you were thinking about or reading for The Reactionary Mind and The Enigma of Clarence Thomas?

Robin: There are some classics that inspired The Reactionary Mind, one of which is The Leopard. But the truth is: there aren’t a lot of great novels on the chaos of reactionary thought, and I think the reason can be found in our society’s vision of politics.

In Britain, Macaulay famously writes, “Government exists for the purpose of keeping the peace.” Compare that to Hegel, in Germany, who writes that “all the worth which a human being possesses, all spiritual reality, he possesses only through the state.” For a lot of Anglo-American political writers, government and politics are limited in scope, an instrument for keeping the peace. I think this is why we’ve had a tough time, particularly in the US, with political novels, whether of the radical or reactionary variety. I don’t think it’s an accident that the greatest political novels in the US are by Black authors, like Morrison and Ellison, for whom politics is closer to what it was for Hegel, that is, for whom it’s clear that politics weighs upon all of our inner lives, our entire spiritual reality.

I wonder how this maps out for you in India. My sense from your novel is that weaving politics into the personal is not nearly as difficult there as it is here. Is that true?

Mahajan: Yes, but that’s because of an inversion of that Macaulay quote about government existing solely to keep the peace. When a government fails at basic tasks, it is suddenly everywhere in the lives of its citizens. To paraphrase Hegel, one’s spirituality is forcibly squeezed through the toothpaste tube of the state. And the history of government in India has been one of massive failures—corruption, infrastructural collapses, bureaucratic delays—which press down on the daily lives of individuals even in the middle and upper classes. Indians are more political because they have no choice but to be political.

Then there’s history. Most people in India are only two or three generations removed from the upheavals of India’s independence and partition. As a Punjabi from Delhi, for example, I can still connect certain social attitudes toward women or Muslims to the violence of partition. American literature would feel quite different if the War of Independence was just in the rearview mirror.

A more cynical part of me worries that the Indian political novel has hardened into a genre—here’s a person, here’s a riot, here’s a sprinkling of postcolonial history. But a genre that attempts to capture the nexus of the personal and the political is preferable, in my mind, to the autobiographical evasions of so much American fiction, which simply replicates the atomization of American life without confronting its causes. Make American writing political again!

entries.title: Eradicating the ‘Fourth Branch’
entries.summary: By ending the independence of federal agencies, the Supreme Court has taken another step toward the creation of an elected presidential dictatorship.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
The recent constitutional revolution at the Supreme Court is the result of a well-coordinated effort over many decades by the conservative legal movement, which has achieved the reversal of a number of high-profile precedents that it excoriated for more than half a century. After the Court’s 2025–2026 term, it’s fair to say that this revolution has reached the end of its beginning. In its first phase, the Court reversed Roe v. Wade in 2022, banned race-based affirmative action in higher education in 2023, and ended so-called Chevron deference to federal agencies’ interpretation of ambiguous legislation in 2024, allowing courts to reverse, for example, long-standing environmental regulations. This year the Court completed the gutting of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, permitting what had long been considered unlawful racial gerrymandering by deeming it constitutionally protected partisan gerrymandering. Then it empowered the president to fire executive branch officials, with the exception of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, for any reason, no matter what laws Congress has made to protect the independence of federal agencies.

All these decisions were bad. All were both predictable and predicted.1 Constricting fundamental rights to liberty, equality, and dignity and empowering a unitary executive who supposedly maintains sole control over the executive branch were central components of the jurisprudence of the late Justice Antonin Scalia, which formed the core of the legal movement from which the current conservative justices all spring.2

The most recent development—the end of agency independence—does not, on the surface, appear to contradict principles held dear by generations of constitutional liberals. There are no social movements that defend or advocate for independent government agencies. Few observers, even among administrative law experts, will find themselves morally exercised by a change in how heads of multimember agencies can be fired.

In practice, however, this technical-sounding change in constitutional interpretation may be even more consequential for government in the United States than the others. The reason is that the Supreme Court has released the executive from the institutional constraints imposed by Congress while the most power-hungry president in US history, Donald Trump, is in the White House. I don’t mean that Trump is now the most powerful president in US history. That honor, dubious or otherwise, still belongs to Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who presided over both a vast expansion of the federal bureaucracy and the creation of the modern US military. I mean that Trump, more than all other presidents, aspires to personalized power unmediated by staff, institutions, norms, or rules and unchecked by independent agencies that Congress created or by Congress itself.

In January 2026 Brendan Carr, President Trump’s handpicked chair of the Federal Communications Commission, announced “competition concerns” regarding a bid by Netflix to acquire Warner Brothers Discovery, the conglomerate that, among other things, owns CNN, the news network that Trump has called “a disgrace,” and CBS, which he has sued. It is not the FCC, however, but the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Justice that are tasked with reviewing the competitiveness consequences of mergers and acquisitions. Carr strongly hinted that the FCC would happily approve a rival bid made by Paramount Skydance, controlled by the Trump ally David Ellison, who since acquiring the parent company of CBS News in 2025 has openly sought to make its editorial policies more Trump-friendly. In April Paramount Skydance’s takeover offer was approved by Warner Brothers’ shareholders. In June the Department of Justice announced that it had no objection to the deal. Twelve state attorneys general sued to block it, then reached a settlement in which Paramount promised to create an “editorial independence board” to set editorial standards for CNN and CBS and resolve conflicts related to the standards. As of this writing, the deal is poised to go through.

Prior to the Trump presidency, it would have been bizarre to the point of unthinkability for the head of an independent agency to intervene so overtly on behalf of the president’s personal interests. But this was not Carr’s first foray into such matters. It was his direct threat to the licensing of ABC affiliates that led the network to take the talk show host Jimmy Kimmel off the air for some weeks in 2025.

What we are seeing is not just some isolated threat to the First Amendment. It is something much deeper: a transformation in the way political power flows through US governance unseen since the New Deal. Not only Trump but his successors, whether Republicans or Democrats, are going to be able to exercise personal authority over the vast apparatus of the federal government in a way that presidents never have before and that was supposed to be foreclosed by the constitutional design of the modern presidency.

Independent agencies were conceived in the late nineteenth century to deliver expert rational policymaking and independent judgment. In their place, we are getting personal rule by personal whim. A president who can fire anyone he hires—the fundamental principle of the unitary executive—is a president who can bend agencies to his will based on personal preference, favoritism, even overt self-enrichment. And because in 2024 the Supreme Court also insulated the president from any criminal consequences for official actions, and because impeachment is now moribund after its twin failures during Trump’s first term, there is nothing anyone can do about it.

Advertisement

The result would be utterly fascinating if it weren’t so horrifying: a historic movement toward caudillo-like presidential power. It is occurring not in a weak democracy like Italy, a former authoritarian state like Hungary, or even a democracy like India with a tradition of near-imperial prime ministerial control, but in the United States, the political scientists’ model of supposedly balanced government. This stands in sharp contrast with the classic Weberian observation that charismatic power gives way to bureaucratized, rationalized institutional power. What we are seeing is something like the opposite: the Supreme Court is actively enabling the transformation of our neo-Madisonian constitutional model of divided government into an elected presidential dictatorship.

Why is this happening? From the standpoint of judicial doctrine, the answer is originalism, the theory that the constitutional order that governs the United States today should be the one that prevailed in 1789 when the Constitution went into effect.

A constitution is meant to be the DNA of a functioning state. If a society undergoes changes and the state does not evolve to adapt to them, it will die—this is the metaphor of the living Constitution, coined by Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes. In 1920 he wrote (in a majority opinion, no less) that the words of the Constitution

called into life a being the development of which could not have been foreseen completely by the most gifted of its begetters. It was enough for them to realize or to hope that they had created an organism; it has taken a century and has cost their successors much sweat and blood to prove that they created a nation.

When Scalia said in a lecture in 2013 that the Constitution is “not a living document” but is “dead, dead, dead,” he thought he was being funny. To his credit, Scalia did have a wicked sense of humor. But the idea of dead constitutionalism is funny only if you don’t take it seriously. The moment you do, the humor dies, and so will the state if its constitutional design does not adapt to a changing world.

Because the Constitution of 1789 includes just three branches of government, originalists have long been perturbed by the existence of the independent administrative agencies created by Congress beginning in 1887 with the Interstate Commerce Commission. The purpose of the ICC, like essentially all the fifty-seven agencies that were affected by the Supreme Court’s recent ruling, was to deploy independent, nonpartisan professional expertise to manage a complex modern economy. The ICC’s mandate, for example, was to regulate railroads and extended over time to include interstate bus lines and early telecoms.

It was plain to Congress that this sort of economic regulation would fail to achieve its goals if it came under the personal control of the president, so it created the agency independence that has been maintained for the past 140 years. The president appoints members of the independent agencies. They must be confirmed by the Senate. Once they are, they serve for fixed terms. The president can fire them only for cause, traditionally understood to mean inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance. While they are in office, they may be subjected to political pressures, but they are largely protected from the vagaries of presidential policy preferences or personal pressure.

This system of balancing was designed to imitate the checks and balances among the legislative, executive, and judicial branches, none of which can do anything meaningful without the input of the others. To anyone who venerates the Madisonian constitutional design, independent agencies were an homage to the genius of mixed government, which adapted and adjusted and evolved during well over half of our history. To the originalists, however, they were an abomination: a “headless ‘fourth branch,’” as critics put it as early as 1937, that has now finally been eradicated.

It is not surprising that the need for independent agencies was not anticipated by the Founders. The Constitution of 1789 envisioned an executive with very little power by today’s standards and a Congress whose power was also far more restricted than it became in the twentieth century (to say nothing of a far weaker Supreme Court). The federal government was relatively weak not only because the United States was so much smaller geographically or because the states were the main sites of political participation. It was because before the Industrial Revolution there was no pressing reason to imagine that the federal government would have to regulate labor, the environment, or even interstate transportation. The original executive branch included just a handful of cabinet secretaries, none of whom commanded an administrative apparatus of any meaningful size. The main executive functions were collecting import duties and conducting foreign affairs, to the extent that that could be done without a substantial standing army or navy.

Advertisement

It was not until after the Civil War that the United States both expanded across the continent and began to industrialize in earnest. The modern administrative state is therefore a creature of an industrial economy operating at continental scale. The establishment of the ICC in 1887 marks as well as anything the moment at which the government of the United States grew up and started governing. The Constitution, in other words, was alive.

This is not the first time that a conservative Supreme Court has wanted to turn back the clock on modern government. As part of the same regulatory effort that gave rise to the administrative state, Congress, beginning in the late nineteenth century, enacted a raft of legislation governing wages, hours, and working conditions. The libertarian-conservative Supreme Court majority of the time ruled much of this legislation unconstitutional as beyond Congress’s power to regulate.

The low point was a child labor case, Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918). Congress had passed a law making it illegal to transport items in interstate commerce that had been manufactured by children under the age of fourteen, or by children between fourteen and sixteen who had been required to work more than eight hours a day, or to work at night, or to work in a mine. The conservative justices struck it down, 5–4, over a blistering dissent by Holmes. It was not until the New Deal and FDR’s threat to pack the Court that the conservative view was swept away—the infamous switch in time that saved nine.

In the 1990s a conservative Supreme Court, influenced by the first flushes of originalist ambition and dominated by Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush appointees, was tempted to reverse the expansive interpretation of Congress’s commerce power that had been accepted for more than half a century. By then the commerce power had become the constitutional basis for most federal law on most subjects. In 1995 the conservative majority struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act on the grounds that it was beyond the power of Congress to bar guns in school, not because of the Second Amendment but because there was not a sufficient connection between school gun violence and interstate commerce. At the time I was in law school, and I can remember my professors’ shock at what looked like the opening salvo of an attempt to roll back modern governmental power.

But after a bit of reflection, the conservatives of that era, including such stalwarts as Chief Justice William Rehnquist, decided that they were unprepared to abandon the basic foundation on which modern federal regulatory power rested. They struck down just one more law, a provision of the Violence Against Women Act, for having exceeded the commerce power.3 In 2005 Scalia himself repudiated this in retrospect incomprehensible effort to dress twenty-first-century government in eighteenth-century garb. In a case challenging the power of Congress to regulate the growing of cannabis for personal use, he voted with the majority to uphold the law. He reasoned that, under the Necessary and Proper Clause of the Constitution, Congress could regulate intrastate activities in order to make the regulation of interstate commerce effective. The Supreme Court’s second assault on the constitutional structure of modern regulation had been averted.

Thwarted from demolishing the entire modern edifice of legislation, the originalists fell back on the supposedly narrower theory known as the unitary executive and turned their attention to using it to undermine the modern administrative state. In this, their third try, they have now succeeded. Independent agencies are no more, with the exception of the Federal Reserve, in a particularly embarrassing form of special pleading. Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh, joined by the Court’s three liberals, took the intellectually indefensible position that the Federal Reserve so closely resembles the First and Second Banks of the United States that it gets a special historical exemption from the powers of the unitary executive that apply to the rest of the government. Their true, highly defensible motivation, revealed by Kavanaugh in a concurrence, was that they did not want to take responsibility for breaking the financial system by destroying Fed independence. The other four conservatives, disinclined to judicial pragmatism in any form, dissented.

Then there is the timing. When Scalia and other jurisprudential conservatives of his generation criticized the power of the administrative state, they were imagining that what they saw as a state run by liberal elites would be supplanted by a Reagan-style executive who would limit government intervention in a roughly libertarian fashion. It never occurred to them that the alternative would be a populist, nakedly corrupt, twice-impeached aspiring dictator who would govern more with the apparent goal of self-aggrandizement than in adherence to any political philosophy.

The disaster being created by today’s conservative justices isn’t motivated by a liking for Trump’s personal style of governance. It’s driven by their blind adherence to the foolish dogma of originalism, regardless of real-world consequences. True, in his first term, Trump appointed three of the conservative justices necessary for the revolution to take place. But he thought he was appointing justices who would be loyal to him personally, and since they have not always ruled in his favor, he considers all three traitors.

What’s unforgivable is that these justices, who cannot be fired by Trump and who believe in the independence of the Supreme Court, appear to think that allowing Trump to fire anyone in the executive branch will not undermine the capacity of the agencies in that branch to govern effectively. The most generous thing you could say about the conservative majority’s decision to end agency independence is that they naively think it won’t have much practical effect. Even among reasonable administrative law experts trying to grasp the insanity of what has just happened, you can hear the hopeful argument that agency independence was never really all that important, given that presidents could ultimately appoint a majority of the members of the independent agencies and thus get their policy preferences carried out.

This view might conceivably have been true in the pre-Trump world, in which presidents expected the people they appointed to run agencies to act on the basis of sound, reasoned judgment rather than personal loyalty or the enrichment of the president and his friends. Yet the fact that Congress sustained the model of agency independence for so long suggests that professional politicians, at least, believe that there’s a difference between directly reporting to a president who can fire you and being appointed by a president who likes your policies but can’t fire you without cause.

Constitutional governance is an experiment, “as all life is an experiment,” Holmes once wrote, quoting Emerson without citation. The purpose of an experiment is to gather data and, on the basis of that experience (note the common root), to ascertain what works and what does not. Agency independence was a crucial part of a fairly successful experiment in modern government in the United States, if success is measured by the country’s wealth and power and the durability of its constitutional structure. Originalism is an experiment in denying experimentation—in perversely refusing the lessons of experience. We will know the consequences soon enough.

—September 24, 2026

entries.content:
In any story by the Scottish writer Ali Smith, you are likely to find a precocious young person who delivers a dose of naked truth, exposing the shams of contemporary mores and politics. You may also find a ghost. These figures often serve as catalysts. They shake other characters awake and chivy them along toward whatever small changes or revelations are possible within the scope of the story. They can be main characters, like the young narrator of Smith’s recent novel Gliff (2024), but more often they turn up unexpectedly, introducing a little wobble in the ongoing narrative, a shade of doubt.

Smith’s ghosts can be driven by the needs of their new, changed condition, as in her second novel, Hotel World (2001), or as transient and unassuming as the floating head of a Victorian child that visits an isolated woman in Winter (2017), a Dickensian touch for a Christmas novel. A ghost may resemble the human it once was, but not wholly. The afterlife strips something from us.

When a dead lover returns in Artful (2012), Smith’s collection of her four semifictional Weidenfeld lectures, she can barely speak or think. She is covered in debris, as if she’d been dropped through the walls of an old house, gathering the detritus of years. The lecture she appears in is called “On Time,” and like other Smith specters, she’s as much a manifestation of the past itself as of a specific person. The bereaved narrator accepts that this weird, grimy version of her lost love is not “real” as we typically understand the term:

I had to congratulate my imagination, for you were very like you. Though I’d never have imagined the imagination could be so good with smell; you smelt quite strong for something or someone imaginary. Either way, you’d come back, and it was about time.

Smith’s ghosts are rarely gloomy—or only intermittently. Death, where is thy sting if we get to hang around incorporeally for a while? They provide the ultimate narrative pivot: Surprise! Still here! And Smith offsets their metaphoric gravitas—their associations with loss, separation, and the riptide of time—with the comic potential of scaring the living or offering pert, disembodied opinions on art. Her ghosts reach back to folklore, but they are also creatures of our dark and boggy present, of our anxieties and disconnection. “I’ve a feeling I’ve inherited them from whatever Scottish literary family I belong to,” she said on the Canadian radio show Bookends.

Smith’s recent paired novels Gliff and Glyph (2026) both feature precocious young siblings. Glyph also has ghosts—and of a type new to Smith’s fiction. One human, one equine, they form what we might call “story ghosts,” the afterimages of powerful stories we can’t process or forget. They haunt as effectively as any jilted bride.

In Gliff, a dystopian novel set in a near-future Britain, two middle-school-aged children, Rose and Briar (Bri), are separated from their mother under mysterious circumstances and abandoned by their mother’s boyfriend, Leif, who may or may not have stolen their passports to sell. The family has been chased from its home by some government body that paints ominous red lines around buildings, cars, and people. Red-lined buildings are slated for demolition and redevelopment; “unverifiable” folk get carted off for reeducation. The hint to move on is unmissable.

In a last act of kindness, Leif brings the siblings to a new town and finds them a stripped nineteenth-century railway worker’s cottage to squat in until his promised return. From this home base, the older sibling, Bri—whose gender is never specified in the novel and who prefers not to be labeled—explores the town, while Rose discovers a group of horses, destined for the knacker, in a field nearby. She befriends a gray gelding and, having learned what the term “abattoir” means, convinces Bri to buy the horse with the last of their money. Rose names him Gliff, since she’d been warned the horse was “gliffy”—hard to handle. This magnificent creature must be concealed but cannot live inside their house for long. For help, they seek out other unverifiable people living secretly at a boarded-up school in town and discover there, among other wonders, a large library and some outmoded but functional computers.

Rose and Bri’s mother, an environmental whistleblower who lives almost as a fugitive, has kept her children away from new technologies and out of the public record. She considers smartphones a liability, not only because they can be tracked—state surveillance is a constant danger in Gliff—but because once you have one, “you see everything through it.” She would prefer her children to learn from the real world. She homeschooled them with her few books; as a result, the siblings share an uncommon knowledge of herbal healing.

Advertisement

Yet Bri is effortlessly “good with machines and tech.” Whenever they get near a laptop they revel in looking up words: “It was always exciting to me the number of things a single word could mean.” Online, then in the school library, they look up “gliff” and find almost two pages of definitions—an incantatory list (both real and fictional) that includes “to glimpse,” “to frighten,” and “to strike a glancing blow at someone or something.” They also try to decipher the Latin motto on the front of the school—Facta sunt ipse verba—marveling that

there was such a thing as a family of words, one that stretched across different languages all touching on each other, hitting or striking each other, acting on each other, influencing each other, agreeing with each other or throwing each other out, disturbing each other, doing all of these things at once.

Bri’s rapture recalls Virginia Woolf’s 1937 essay “Craftmanship,” a small section of which, taped for the BBC, constitutes the only surviving recording of her plummy Edwardian voice. (Its centering diphthongs, a feature now confined to a few well-heeled nonagenarians, make “survive” verge on three syllables.) Words, Woolf wrote in that essay, “are the wildest, freest, most irresponsible, most unteachable of all things.” The difficulty in modern writing, she argued, is that old words are “so stored with meanings, with memories” that they are hard to combine with new words: they have already “contracted so many famous marriages.”

Smith’s characters frequently swoon over dictionaries, but Woolf would have disapproved: “Words do not live in dictionaries; they live in the mind.” She resented the constraints (and exclusions) of the great institutions and their codifiers. Her father edited the Dictionary of National Biography and was an early reader for the Oxford English Dictionary: one reason why, to Woolf, a dictionary was a patriarchal rule book—and not even a complete or impartial one.1

In compiling The Book Lover (2006), a collection of excerpts from some of her favorite and formative reading, Smith realized so many came from Woolf that “maybe this would have to be a Woolf anthology.” Aside from their feminism and stylistic affinities, they both write in service of books, libraries, and the freedom to read. Even Smith’s metaphors are often based on books and language; when a teenager, Magnus, falls in love with a charismatic interloper in her novel The Accidental (2005), he feels “she had entered him like he was water. Like he was a dictionary and she was a word he hadn’t known was in him.”

Smith loves to consider etymologies and their cultural implications. Almost all her novels include etymologies, which she uses as pivots—a way in, a way out, a thematic expansion—and as washes of unexpected color. In a 2025 interview with NPR, she was asked about an early job writing advertising copy for her brother’s business. Her memories of a biscuit jingle she came up with spark a meditation on the word “slogan”:

It’s connected to the English word slughorn, because it comes from a Gaelic word that sounds more like sluggern. And sluggern and slughorn meant a war cry. So slogans are directly descended from warfare and war cries—the noise that one tribe makes when it’s facing another and it blows its horn going [imitating horn blowing]. Buy Paterson Bronte Golden Crunch, the perfect fireside snack [imitating horn blowing]. Almost everything about slogans can be connected to the tribal in us, which is why they work so well.2

In Gliff it is hard not to see her brainy youths as self-portraits, especially when Bri rushes to share their list of definitions for “gliff” with Rose: “See, listen, you’ve actually called him something unpindownable. Something really excitingly polysemous…. Polysemous. I looked that word up too.” Not only Smith’s formal experiments but her constant wordplay, punning, and riffing give her prose a sense of superabundance, of endless, rapid-fire invention held back—sometimes belatedly—by her perception that she has taken her reader too far into the ether. Smith wrote her doctoral dissertation on the ordinary in modernist literature, so the balance between what Woolf called “granite and rainbow” (the solidity of “truth” or material reality and the insubstantial qualities of personality or emotion) has long been on her mind.3

Smith was born in Inverness in 1962, the youngest (by six years) of five children in a working-class family. Her father was an electrician and contractor with a gift for storytelling, and her mother helped in his shop. Neither parent was able to complete school, but they prized education for their children. The Smiths had only two artworks in the house, one a well-known print of bluebell woods that her mother could not resist and that her father thought a waste of money. When Smith evokes her mother’s ghost in a recent art catalog for the Munch Museum, So in the Spruce Forest (2025), she gives her a penetrating critical sensibility, restoring an art education she had never had:

Advertisement

Then the voice from nowhere carried on talking about Munch, like my mother of all people knew about Munch, like she knew I was looking at a picture right now, like she knew about the power crisis and the international unrest and the climate ruination in a world she’d left thirty years ago. Like she knew it all.

It was lovely to hear her voice again.

As a child Smith read her siblings’ schoolbooks and later realized she had absorbed much of the canon (Joyce, Orwell, Swift) before the age of ten. Almost as important were the two cinemas in town, one of which showed foreign films on weekends. When Smith digresses in her fiction, she often writes about representation, about how stories and films work; near the middle of The Accidental is a two-page tour de force on cinema, a floating first-person account of the filmic formation of some collective, unnamed narrator whose experiences are shared almost universally. “My mother was a nun who could no longer stand the convent,” we learn.

She married my father, the captain; he was very strict. She taught us all to sing and made us new clothes out of curtains….

When I was a child I ran the Grand National on my horse. They didn’t know I was a girl until I fainted and they unbuttoned my jockey shirt.

Glyph, for its part, pulls in many of the narrative beats from Laurel and Hardy’s Wrong Again (1929), in which the hapless duo brings a horse inside.

Smith studied English at the University of Aberdeen and went on to Newnham College, Cambridge, for a Ph.D. There she met her future partner, Sarah Wood—a filmmaker and artist and Smith’s frequent collaborator—when Wood directed a play of hers. Smith taught English and American literature for eighteen months at the University of Strathclyde in Glasgow, but she felt alienated by the changes occurring in academia, including the recasting of universities as businesses. She developed chronic fatigue syndrome at twenty-seven and took months to recover. As she later put it, “I had to stop so that I could decide which road to cross.” She returned to Cambridge, where she wrote the stories in her first book, Free Love and Other Stories (1995), which won the Saltire First Book of the Year Award.

Her debut novel, Like, followed two years later. Like’s autobiographical elements include aspects of the class divide and the unequal relationship between Scotland and England. Smith introduces some of the doubling and layering that build in her later work. Timelines weave. Fire is a recurrent theme; one of the main characters goes by Ash, short for Aisling. In retrospect, the novel is also about the closet, about the displacement and destruction that result when two girls can’t just love each other.

Four of Smith’s novels have been short-listed for the Booker, but her most celebrated book is probably How to Be Both (2014), her sixth novel, composed of two separate but interconnected narratives set five hundred years apart. It was published in two versions, each beginning with one of those narratives. (Smith’s publisher split the print run in half; the covers were identical.) One part of How to Be Both features a dead narrator, the Quattrocento painter Francesco del Cossa (secretly a cross-dressing girl in this novel), who finds himself “shot back into being like an arrow [to] find myself now in this intermediate place.” Cossa really existed but left almost no biographical record—a perfect opportunity to invent one. The other part is a contemporary story in which a woman drags her adolescent daughter to Ferrara to see the enchanting frescoes Cossa painted with Cosmè Tura at the Palazzo Schifanoia (the Palace of Escape from Boredom).

Smith’s work takes a darker turn after How to Be Both, reflecting the political turmoil of the past ten years, especially the refugee crisis, climate change, and new legal restrictions on free expression and street protest. Her seasonal quartet, which begins with Autumn (2016) and ends with Summer (2020), is both a love letter to nature and art and a counterpunch to the rise of the far right.4 She intended the quartet to be about longevity, she said in an interview with The Paris Review, “and, at the same time, about the surface of whatever was happening in the world at the time the book was being written.”

They do function as state-of-Britain novels, though their sociopolitical concerns will feel familiar across the globe. Also familiar are the stupid bureaucratic snarls that arise from tighter regulations (at the bank, at the post office, at the passport bureau), the sense of everything getting worse and harder, and of our collective exhaustion at constant loss, shock, and forced adjustment. When a character in Spring (2019) visits his dying friend, he asks, “How’re you doing, apart from the end of liberal capitalist democracy?” Spring could serve as a sister novel to Gliff, with its gifted young person—this one a bit magical, to suit the season—and its underground network of rescuers, its stubborn assertion that kindness can still change the world.

Gliff, which won the 2026 Dublin Literary Award, began as a short story commissioned for an anthology of Kafka-inspired fiction, A Cage Went in Search of a Bird (2024). That story, “Art Hotel,” unseated the novel Smith had been working on and, lightly edited, became the opening chapters of Gliff. The bureaucratic menace of Kafka’s 1925 The Trial looms over the unverifiables of the novel, but its presiding spirit is Orwell, who would recognize the double life Bri constructs as the plot develops: a sliver of authenticity and remembered happiness sealed off from their outward conformity to an authoritarian system. In that hidden self lies Bri’s tenacious bond with Rose, long after circumstances drive Rose and Gliff away from her.

It sounds flip to describe Gliff as Smith’s glyphosate novel, but her wordplay in the homophone titles Gliff and Glyph is intentional. In between the publications of the two novels, the UK license for glyphosate, the chemical used in herbicides like Roundup, was extended until mid-December 2026, although its toxicity and environmental dangers are well documented.5 While pregnant with Rose, Bri’s mother had written public relations copy for the weed killer conglomerate Kindweed, trying to convince buyers of its safety. She tells Bri that a former employee, a chemist, confided that the weed killer “didn’t just poison weeds and grasses and flowers and insects, but was also unsafe for lots of other bigger living things. Including dogs, and birds, and cows, and the milk that came from them.” And horses, we assume, as well as humans, especially children and developing fetuses. The product marketed as Kindweed’s gentlest is secretly the same as the company’s most virulent. When Bri’s mother began quietly asking questions, she was sacked.

The relationship between Gliff and Glyph is like a set of mirrors installed at irregular angles, the last of which reflects something outside. Themes are repeated, including the sibling bond. Other correspondences flash and fade. The news is ominous and true to life—AI takeover, economic collapse—but Glyph has a tonal shift, a puckish quality that feels more characteristic of Smith’s earlier fiction than Gliff does. The plot centers on two middle-aged sisters, Petra and Patricia (“Patch”) Wild, who have barely spoken after the bruising experience of sorting their dead parents’ possessions eight years earlier. They shared a tense childhood; after their loving mother died young, their father, prone to outbursts, withdrew into angry silence when not punishing Petra, the elder of the two. A few pages into Glyph, we learn that Gliff is a speculative dystopian novel that Patch has sent Petra as an olive branch. Patch’s foster daughter, Billie, had been reading it, “phone usually glued to the hand but for three whole days it was nothing but a book.”

What really caught Patch’s eye was the title. When the sisters were young, not long before their mother died, Petra invented a ghost—or rather, pretended to contact one in order to comfort Patch. The girls had heard a real-life horror story from World War II about a corpse found flattened on a road in France, as if run over and over by a convoy of tanks, and Patch couldn’t sleep afterward. Petra pretends to ring up the flattened man, who is fine in the afterlife: “He said that he doesn’t really like being reminded of what happened to him but that you thinking of him had made him very moved and pleased.” They were both, Petra suggests, “to go to sleep now and wake up tomorrow free from worry.” Patch believes and disbelieves in this phone call with the dead. But the ghost, instead of remaining a onetime “jeu d’esprit,” as Petra’s worried mother calls him, sticks around, becoming real enough to name. They call him “Glyph.”

Once Gliff stirs the memory of their ghost, Petra feels a surge of guilt, the clear

wrongness in what we were doing, using a terrible true story, the ghost or the shade of a story, about something abysmal that I’m assuming really did happen to someone real, to distract ourselves from feeling what we must no doubt have been feeling, and sensing, round what turned out to be—and look at me now even in this sentence still keeping it at a distance—our mother’s impending death.

As the only redress she can imagine, she launches an extensive online search to try to find anything “real and true” about the dead man. But her thoughts are interrupted by bouts of clattering noise in her house, as if her neighbor were throwing furniture. And what is that smell? She finally throws open a door to find a spectral horse tearing apart her bedroom. Petra’s first call is to Patch, to lay a ghost (or two) to rest and try to mend their estrangement.

The wartime story at the heart of Glyph originates with the writer Xandra Bingley, Smith’s former agent. A member of Bingley’s family had encountered the flattened corpse on a road in the south of France near the end of the war. “Someone tells you something and it goes into you like osmosis,” Smith told an interviewer on the BBC radio show Take Four Books. “And I have not been able to stop thinking about this for a long time.” She had the story in mind while writing Gliff, but she “couldn’t actually face it. I couldn’t get near it. I couldn’t get to the kind of horrific quality of the removal of dimension from the human being. I couldn’t get near it until…I’d written the first book.”

In Glyph, Petra watches what seems like Gaza coverage on television while completing a Duolingo lesson on her phone. Increasingly, in Smith’s work, technology has been tied to the question of witnessing and to our increasing numbness to suffering. A character in Winter realizes she “had been feeling nothing for some time now. Refugees in the sea. Children in ambulances. Blood-soaked men running to hospitals or away from burning hospitals carrying blood-covered children.” In How to Be Both, a teenager is traumatized by accidentally clicking on a website displaying a child rape. She vows never to turn away from abuse, never to choose anesthesia.

In Regarding the Pain of Others (2003), Susan Sontag argued that visual depictions of suffering could diminish lived experience and risked becoming mere aesthetic objects, especially if displayed in a gallery or museum. Private viewing might preserve the emotional effect, she thought. She could not have foretold the bovine trance in which we scroll past hundreds of images a day on our own tiny screens.

Many of Smith’s novels have addressed the rise of consumer technologies. As early as There but for the (2011), she brilliantly described Google search as a “whole new way of feeling lonely,” with its

semblance of plenitude but really a new level of Dante’s inferno, a zombie-filled cemetery of spurious clues, beauty, pathos, pain, the faces of puppies, women and men from all over the world tied up and wanked over in site after site, a great sea of hidden shallows.

Terrible things also happen to books in Smith’s work. For a writer so fiercely supportive of public libraries and so dreamily susceptible to what the diarist W.N.P. Barbellion called the “almost audible susurrus of desire—the desire every book has to be taken down and read,” Smith seems to enjoy mangling them. One character in an early story tears out the pages of her books one by one as she finishes reading them. Like ends with a shocking conflagration, though books are punished throughout, perhaps made to bear their young writer’s anxieties of authorship. Or it may be that familiarity does breed contempt—or at least overwhelm, as those with book heaps can attest. At a bookstore event to promote So in the Spruce Forest, Wood and Smith described leaving a book outside to see how the elements worked on it.6 They think it was The Tempest.

Smith is gentler to books in Gliff and Glyph, however, as if they are friends down on their luck. In Glyph, a book reconnects estranged siblings—a reminder of a shared literary culture we used to idealize (like a tidal island, not always reachable from the mainland). And in Gliff, with its wondrously preserved school library, we revisit the mind-expanding potential of books, the radical freedom they embody as freedom recedes elsewhere: “Wherever my eye went, books. Oh! I said.”

entries.title: The Elusive Glamour of Peter and Paul
entries.summary: A dual biography of Peter Hujar and Paul Thek is a tantalizing portrait of the artists and their epoch, just before the catastrophe of AIDS.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Peter Hujar and Paul Thek never look happier, together or apart, than in a photo of them side by side on Fire Island in 1961. Tall and lean in swimming trunks, with the sea behind them, both men are reacting to something out of shot, Thek smiling sweetly, while Hujar, who is hairier and rather more muscular, grins widely and bares his long upper gums in a way that I don’t think is seen in any other photo of him. It gives us a moment of intimate access, sixty-five years later, to a Peter Hujar who is otherwise unknown to us, the man Thek knew, and loved. The happiness was real, for a time, but the two artists, each with his own distinct problems and needs, were not going to be happy together, or with anyone else, for long. Both found loving difficult, Thek with recurrent uncertainties about his sexuality—he slept with Susan Sontag, their close friend at the time, and talked of wanting to have a child with her. Hujar’s personal reserve was clearly a part of his appeal, a magnetic reticence, but it betokened a deeper inability to give himself. And besides, was romantic happiness, conventionally conceived, what either man wanted?

To read an individual, or a milieu, through photographs can be, at its best, to see deep and to know how fragile the chance of such a revelation was; the caught moment endures to reveal, to typify, and to invite interpretation. In The Wonderful World That Almost Was, Andrew Durbin reaches several times for the never-quite-explicable nature of the camera’s insights, both the subject’s experience of being acutely seen and the viewer’s conviction of access to a person they may otherwise know little or nothing about. He describes how in Hujar’s early photos of his teacher Daisy Aldan we see her slip free of self-consciousness into “an almost revelatory inner state”; Hujar’s friend Ann Wilson spoke of his “gorgeous mental discretion”—an openness of vision and an instinct for selection—which uncovered “the inmost selves of his subjects.” This is the magic of good portraiture in any medium, but the instantaneous analysis of the camera is the more uncanny, and it’s clear that for the troubled and often taciturn Hujar, photography was a vital means of engagement not only with the larger world but with his own inner being. In his many photographs of Thek over nearly two decades he found, Durbin feels, a kind of revelation, an understanding of “unseen parts of himself.” Even someone who has not had the wrenching experience of reading his book would surely find these portraits exceptionally moving.

The two men had met five years earlier in Florida, when each was with a different partner, and Hujar’s first photos of Thek, in and around a house in Coral Gables, are the record of a coolly charged encounter between an unknown twenty-three-year-old artist and an uncannily attentive photographer a year younger than him. Thek perches on a spindly sofa in a bare-floored room, with an array of potted plants in front of the window; he is obliging but not passive, and seems hemmed in, an outdoor creature domestically confined; his long legs stretch out in front of him, then he’s barefoot and sitting on the floor. We can’t help but read his expression through the lens of hindsight—it seems by turns questioning, seductive, and opaque. Out of the house, in white shorts, he reclines on the ground in a pine glade, where Hujar too is photographed against the trees. The youthful softness of both young men, Hujar dark, Thek fairer, is very notable, and it’s a heightened and inexorable feature of this particular story that we will watch them as they age and are weathered by difficult and in the end fatal experience.

Durbin’s absorbing and original book is a joint biography, a vividly detailed account of the years the two men were part of each other’s lives, though for much of that time not together. He keeps their two stories on the move, intertwines them when he can, and produces a narrative as hard to summarize as life itself. The childhood years, rich in significance for both men, are quickly dealt with, six pages for Hujar and five for Thek. This skipping over material a traditional biographer might have raked through in detail is a little disconcerting, though the determining facts emerge clearly. Thek was born in 1933 in Brooklyn to a German father and an Irish mother and grew up from the age of seven in Floral Park on Long Island, in a casually Catholic household, with three siblings. What their father’s job was is not stated, though it took him “gray-suited” to the city, and his discovery of Paul’s homosexuality made relations between them lastingly difficult; in his father’s absence his mother developed a heavy reliance on drink.

Advertisement

Hujar, born in 1934 in Trenton, New Jersey, was also the child of an alcoholic mother, a waitress; he had no memory of his absconded father and was brought up on the farm of his mother’s parents, who were Ukrainian—Ukrainian was apparently his first language. Anyone who has spent time on a farm as a child will feel the subtle force of his many later photographs of cows and horses, the sense of sought-for solidarity and proximate friendship with nonhuman neighbors. At the age of eleven he was sent back to live with his mother and her new husband, a bookie, in a one-bedroom apartment on East 32nd Street; his habits of watchful silence, the lack of love and fear of loving, the anger that came with powerlessness, all seem to stem from these formative years. In adult life his rages would be terrifyingly violent, at times nearly murderous; his friend Vince Aletti said he was “the angriest person I knew”; Fran Lebowitz, also a close longtime friend, thought he “never learned to be in the world, not one bit”—a child’s bewilderment that persisted in the grown-up artist and was a key to the decades-long quest of his work.

Both men died of AIDS-related illnesses, Hujar in November 1987, nine months before Thek. Durbin’s intention is to tell their story, to create his own portrait of the time they shared, with no premonition of the catastrophe that awaited them and their world. The last decade of their separate lives is covered in ten pages. The effect is again startling, but unusually akin to the understanding we may have in real life of those we meet in adulthood, are close to for a while, and then lose touch with, their prior and subsequent stories a matter of anecdote, of random news and reported sightings. The poignancy of the book stems in part from the messiness and irresolution of the narrative, and also from Durbin’s proper reluctance to force form on the struggles of two such conflicted and often unaccommodating characters, who for the greater part of their lives had nothing to do with each other. But the result is also tantalizing, leaving you hungry for a fuller account of Thek’s life in particular: you worry about him as you might about a self-destructive friend you’re unable, in the end, to help.

Durbin was born not long after his subjects died, and he is understandably magnetized by their epoch, astonishing for its claiming of new freedoms, its roil of political optimism and disillusion, and the pervasive possibility, central to his story, of seizing chances for change, for personal metamorphosis and growth. It has too the glamour of a legendary party that he missed, and at which his book will make him magically an observer, and almost a participant. His tone at times is that of someone less researching than remembering a particular scene, the brilliant people, the talk and the laughter, the dancing till dawn in long-vanished clubs. At moments he’s recalling the larger mood of the time: “There was always something incongruous and contradictory about gay relationships in the early part of the decade.” Then he’s up close with his principals: “It was the way Paul stared at you, as if his absorbing blue eyes were endowed with X-ray powers. Just made you swoon.”

He has a keen sense of the physical presence and sexiness of both men. In his Cooper Union yearbook Thek was “the boy with the most beautiful eyes,” and later his “sensuous power” is acknowledged and takes on a symbolic charge: “The era itself emanated from his body: The 1960s felt of Paul, and Paul the 1960s.” We learn too (a rare thing in biography) of his “beautiful voice,” “his most seductive device.” But it’s Hujar whom Durbin seems keener on. “Of course, he was beautiful,” he writes, with “a smile that could make anything look sexy” and a “beautiful face.” He has contemporary support for this: “Men and women found him terribly handsome,” and Hujar’s friend Sheyla Baykal described him as “so beautiful, tall. Intense. Intelligent looking.” Readers can study the many self-portraits and work out what they feel about him; it’s the frank physical admiration of male author for male subject that’s refreshing, and a part of the book’s immersive feel.

A more conventional approach might occasionally have been useful. The artist Ann Wilson is knocking around in the story, like the good friend she was, for nearly two hundred pages before Durbin formally introduces her and tells us how she and Hujar met; in Rome, where Hujar had gone on a Fulbright in 1962, Cy Twombly and Federico Fellini are abruptly good friends to the two younger artists; others, minor figures in a scene fast receding into the past, bob in and out as if we really should know who they are. Indeed a latent motif of the book, to do with fame and transience, seems encoded in the fleeting presence of these unexplained actors and dancers. Durbin falls back on unsupported presumptions—as in “The ancient sculpture must have caught Paul’s eye”—surprisingly rarely, considering the mysteries of his two subjects’ thoughts and experiences, but he often speaks for them, or through them. “Paul’s love could make you feel light, a lightness Peter craved in most romantic relationships.” “Love was power and torment for Paul, and for Peter, a temporary relief.” “Seeing them filled their friends with wonder, and even a little envy, that two people could really be so close.” This is on the romantic, novelistic side of biography, though such interpretative touches form part of a consistent and convincing whole.
