Of the two artists, Hujar has the photographer’s obvious advantage: his work is widely reproduced, and much of it is now internationally known, from exhibitions, books, and online archives. Though some of his major breakthroughs occurred in Italy, he is above all a New York photographer, born halfway between Diane Arbus, who he felt looked down on him, and Robert Mapplethorpe, unmentioned in Durbin’s book though described by him elsewhere as Hujar’s “long-time nemesis…whose work he often mocked and dismissed”*; in the Morgan Library’s exhibition “Hujar:Contact,” he’s glimpsed, leather-jacketed in a bar, in 1981. If Hujar can at moments be compared with both these more famous figures, his empathetic portraiture could rarely be confused with theirs. Certainly his early photos of children in an orthopedic hospital in Florence have a radiant sense of communicated tenderness and joy that sets them apart from Arbus’s work; when he took them, Hujar was traveling with an earlier boyfriend, the painter Joseph Raffael, who was in Italy on his own Fulbright scholarship, and a sense of displacement in a strange country surely precipitates new insight into the “richness of the children’s inner lives.” His pictures of two leathermen, Jay and Fernando, making out in 1967 seem a forerunner of Mapplethorpe’s Bobby and Larry Kissing twelve years later, but for Durbin these are only preparatory stages in Hujar’s development, studies of a sexual type, lacking the personal insight that would characterize his later, often more explicit sex photos. The aesthetic, monumental, almost abstract nature of Mapplethorpe’s treatment of the male body was not to be Hujar’s way.

He did copious commercial work to get by, most significantly as chief assistant in Harold Krieger’s busy Midtown studio between 1964 and 1968. Here he developed, in parallel and after hours, his own obsessions with light and with the ways, very different from posing a fashion model, that the essence of an individual might be captured. The brilliance of his portraits lay always in finding a connection that bypassed the routine and artificial contract of the sitting. This was a two-way thing, and unpredictable. In Ira Sachs’s film Peter Hujar’s Day (2025), based on transcripts of a conversation with his friend Linda Rosenkrantz in 1974, he’s frustrated by a shoot with Allen Ginsberg for The New York Times: “There’s very little there…. It’s not that he didn’t give out. We didn’t connect”; and indeed the photo, of Ginsberg sitting cross-legged in an abandoned shop doorway, straight on but with eyes askance, distinctly conveys a lack of shared purpose, the all-too-common scenario of making do for a press deadline.

The opposite occurs in an outdoor shoot with Roberto Rossellini six years earlier, which takes rich advantage of a group of kids playing in an urban park, mere happenstance that both director and photographer yield to and explore: the children’s excitement at being in the picture infects the large, balding, suited Rossellini, and he stands smiling among them, surprised, amused, and above all in a live communication with Hujar. The children are not exploited for effect but are participants in a cheerfully impromptu occasion with unexpected rewards. It would be more and more the case that Hujar flourished artistically as the recorder of his own milieu of artists, writers, and especially performers: the reticent observer reveling in the performative exuberance of others.

To Durbin, he is “one of the greatest American portraitists of all time.” And his work extended beyond portraiture: to be in downtown New York through the 1970s was to move in a city in physical decay, and he had long been a feeling recorder of urban dereliction, seeing in it both the trace (enigmatic, amusing, sad) of what had gone and the lurking promise of the life that thrived in the ruins. There’s a palpable tension in these empty downtown streets and abandoned buildings, a nervy expectation in the shadows. His studies of men cruising on the abandoned West Side piers are in their way both townscapes and portraits, the artist’s habit of seeing and his search for sex fused in a complex image of a time and a place where everyone is on the lookout.

Compared to Hujar’s memorable body of work, Thek’s is more elusive and its status more uncertain. A fair bit of it was destroyed, sometimes thrown out from his New York apartment during his absences in Europe, crises that he typically found liberating and regenerative; other sculptural works, installations and “environments,” intrinsically more ephemeral, are harder to assess. The extreme variety of his creative work speaks to irresolvable dualities, pluralities, in his own nature: on the Italian island of Ponza, a favored retreat, he produced exquisitely fine landscape drawings, much as other northern artists in the Mediterranean world had been making for centuries; in Norway, in Italy, or on Fire Island he was a rapturous recorder in fairly conventional means of the beauties of sea, sunlight, and the life of the body; in a tower in Sicily he fixated on painting a sequence of black-and-white Television Analyzations—for example, a woman’s neck and chin seen in close-up on a TV screen; while for shows in Italy, Holland, and New York he produced simulations in wax of bleeding meat and severed body parts, so realistic that they made many viewers “sick to their stomachs.” Some of these were exhibited in Technological Reliquaries, sleekly modernist vitrines of yellow-tinted Plexiglass, which only made them more sinister. Later, in the years beyond Durbin’s detailed study, his paintings were increasingly centered on words and slogans—“diligence,” “HURRAH VACUII,” “Afflict the comfortable COMFORT THE AFFLICTED”—which can seem rather private and profitless after what had come before.

Durbin recounts how the installations were set up, at (or sometimes after) the last minute, with the help of collaborators, eloquent fusions of the improvised and the fiercely determined. In The Tomb a cast of Thek’s own body, assembled Frankenstein-wise in many parts, lies in jeans and a double-breasted jacket, the entire figure, except for the long blond wig and mustache, painted a pale lilac pink. Its purple tongue protrudes, as if waiting, perhaps, to receive the sacrament. Nicknamed “the Hippie,” it was displayed at the Stable Gallery on East 74th Street in 1967, laid out with various grave goods inside a carpentered pink pyramid with a single entrance for the nervous viewer to peer in. A photo in The Village Voice showed Thek, looking fit and well, posing in the tomb beside his 3D image of his own corpse. This ritual offering was perhaps a further liberation—he had staged his own funeral and was free to move on—while the work unsurprisingly attracted widespread interpretation, both personal and political. It was a protest against American state violence, at home and abroad; it was a memorial to the idealism of a young artist and a critique of the culture in which he had tried to thrive.

Durbin reckons this lost installation a “masterpiece of 1960s American sculpture,” and his descriptions of it, and of Thek’s work in various media, are all the more welcome in this sadly underillustrated book (one central gathering of small black-and-white images, two or three to the page, as in any conventional biography published in the past sixty years). You have to keep turning to online resources and to other books. Paul Thek: Diver, the large volume connected to the Whitney’s retrospective of his work fifteen years ago, is the most useful guide I’ve found to reconstructing a partly lost corpus: it documents how things were and shows what survives. And part of the interest of a lovely exhibition, “Paul Thek: Seized by Joy,” at the Thomas Dane Gallery in London last summer was that it combined some rich early landscapes and still lifes painted on newspaper (a recurrent support, both for thrift and for its symbolic transience) with large luminous watercolors from the 1980s, the years after Durbin’s main narrative ends. Fire Island vistas, charged with Thek’s lifelong hunger for the sea and its shore, hung alongside atmospheric views from his apartment window of smokestacks and water tanks against the sunset.

Two photos capture moments of ambiguous calm. One, a composite by Lou Zeldis, shows him just two months before his death, perched on his sunny rooftop amid dozens of pots of orange cosmos. The Manhattan skyline, part famous, largely anonymous, stretches into the blue beyond. He wears a white tank top, as he does in Hujar’s color photo in 1966 in their shared house on Fire Island, where he sits at his newsprint-covered worktable strumming his guitar, sheet music open beside him, while a line of dismembered pink hands (with a few individual fingers and thumbs) seems to scuttle away along the ledge behind him (see illustration on page 21).

Hujar, it’s clear, wasn’t a writer. “Correspondence placed demands upon Peter that his more fluent and expressive friends could probably barely imagine,” Durbin explains. But Thek was a voluble, needy, and at his best wonderfully eloquent letter writer, and happily the costive Hujar preserved all that he received. The large album Stay away from nothing is unprefaced, unindexed, unannotated, with only a two-page afterword by Durbin to give background to what we’ve read. It is made up mainly of facsimiles of Thek’s letters from Holland or Sicily or Ponza to Hujar in Rome or back in the US, most of them tightly typed to use all the space, others handwritten, sometimes in capital letters. The nearly weightless aerograms, now creased and crumpled, are reproduced on heavier stock, but we have the experience of seeing exactly the page that Thek typed, folded, sealed with the tip of his tongue along its gummed edges, and mailed, and that a week or so later Hujar carefully snicked open and read. We are the proxy recipients of these letters, stopping and squinting at times to make them out, and their articulated ecstasies, bewilderments, and plunges into drug-muddled craziness bring us into an intimate relation with Thek of a kind we will never so explicitly have with Hujar. Small gatherings of Hujar’s photographs of him mark the times they were together and add haunting eloquence to the more stumbling disclosure, across the fifteen years of Thek’s letters, of decline and alienation.

The highs are exhilarating, a postwar American version of the young artist finding himself in Europe but excited less by the antique world than by isolation in wild places, islands, and mountains. The elation begins on the first long crossing by sea in 1962, “the most exciting week of my life,” young Paul up in the crow’s nest with a 360-degree view, “like flying in all directions at once…and the magnificence goes round and round in my little head.” Physical sensation, and the interest of new places, are nonetheless secondary to his need to work, and to find a space of his own in which to do it. It’s beautiful being in Amsterdam, “but when all is said and done, I do still prefer work”—“I want to set up a studio, with orange juice, and live.” It turns out that Rome in the mid-1960s contains not just ruins, churches, and palaces but a happening and open-minded contemporary art scene, more welcoming to him than the one back home. Twombly and Fellini are indeed at work there, among many others. The Roman gallerist Topazia Alliata lends Thek a medieval tower in the village of Casteldaccia in northern Sicily, and there he seems to enter into the life of the artist in a rapturous new way. Solitude, not yet a threat, is part of it, mitigated by the adoption of a cat he names Gattopardo, after Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa’s great Sicilian novel. The words “happy” and “happiness” radiate through the letters, the happiness of a found routine in a place with its own immemorial seasonal life:

Again a lemon picking walk in the groves, one of the sweetest deepest happinesses of my life, tears in the eyes, what a tramonto! and everything glowing in that special Redon way, the air so filled with tiny radiating spectrums, like millions of prisms, the terraces going on hill after hill, thrusting themselves quickly forward in that special Italian way of changing landscape…. Tears in the eyes, lemons in the busta and in the pockets, if only I had another month to work here.

The rapture seems perilous in the light of what is to come. The crow’s-nest, tower-top highs are followed by a bumpy and protracted descent, the long-sought solitude becoming its own problem. Four years later, in Rome on his own Fulbright (these a critical motor of both men’s stories), he feels he should hang out with friends, but “I gotta be me I gotta be me”: people “drive me mad I can never give them what they want” (and gaps now replace punctuation). Feelings of inadequacy and paranoia deepen with his heavy intake of hash. “I am frequently stoned,” he says the following winter, and he seems increasingly unable to separate the delusions from the revelations of being so. “Apparantly Im supposed to be reborn or something,” he writes, a fuddled grasp for a lifelong principle. He grows needier, repeatedly asking Hujar to send him random things—money, butterfly wings for an artwork, sunscreen, weight-loss pills—and like most very stoned people he starts to get boring, the verbal brio dimmed. In Amsterdam again he’s on meds and seems normal, “though them that know me better know me better…a messier mind you couldn’t hardly find.”

His sexual feelings, often colored by residual Catholic guilt, perplex him. In Sicily he’d had a fantasy of being married to a woman (whom he imagines mostly as a servant) and existed “almost as if not homosexual”; now, in 1968, he’s “much much closer” with Sontag in Stockholm, though dryly mocking when Joseph Raffael turns straight and gets married. “I think hell make a very nice heterosexual,” he writes, asserting that “queer has a purpose and it seems morally wrong to me to not sleep with ones own sex too…. Hedonism and love are the only way.” There are mad exaltations—“My head is filled with wings and saints as always and there is no longer any reason to resist any of it as I am not involved other than as a receiver of gifts”—and times when you don’t know if he’s genuinely adrift or drolly self-aware. In Ponza in a sailboat in 1969: “Somehow want to do the Red Sea wherever that is I have a feeling it will work out.” Three years later, in Essen in West Germany: “I think I’ve gone mad 2 or 3 times by now, if it matters…. Please let us love each other…. Living so personalized, individualized, is becoming unbearable.”

Hujar’s later studies of him are unbearable too, in their transcendent way: wild-haired and bearded on the Fire Island shore in 1973, and neater, with a gaze both lost and challenging, in their final shoot two years later, which seems also to have been the occasion of their last significant meeting. This was for the only book of his work that Hujar was to publish, Portraits in Life and Death (1976), which presented twenty-nine images of artists, actors, and writers, including Sontag, who wrote an introduction, followed by eleven photos from the visit he and Thek had paid to the Capuchin catacombs in Palermo thirteen years earlier, where the preserved but slowly decaying corpses made a profound impression on both young men.

Throughout his biography, Durbin gives illuminating readings of many photographs, and of the masterly work Hujar did in the darkroom to manipulate an image and enrich its meaning; “Hujar:Contact” gives us further ways to explore the contingency of a shoot and the decisions that followed. The Hujar archive at the Morgan Library houses more than 5,700 contact sheets, some 110 of which are included in the exhibition, as well as the numbered job books in which he logged his shoots; as Joel Smith suggests—in the first of the brilliant short essays that punctuate the catalog—they are the closest we will ever get to a memoir by Hujar himself, a record not only of whom and what he photographed, but of the process of selection that is fundamental to creating art. Readers of the book, like visitors to the show, will want a jeweler’s loupe to read the tiny detail of the sheets, from which, once in awhile, an image is pulled out and enlarged full page. It’s an absorbing, almost magical experience. In the digital age, as Smith says, “the format of the analog contact sheet [has] a special romance of its own”—sometimes a record of rapid stabs at a subject over the twelve exposures of a roll of film, sometimes more pondered approaches to a sitter across a longer timespan. The selected “timeless” portrait can be seen among all the other shots at it—a sequence of distracting and promising possibilities.

The range of subjects is amazing in itself; if the book is a memoir by proxy it is also a portrait of an era. One of the keen insights Hujar derived from his growing interest in the group and the scene was the way a person reveals himself or herself in reaction to others; an individual portrait might result not from a traditional solo sitting but from homing in on one figure in a group shoot. His orange crayon isolates Raffael from a group of ten other artists and staff at the Stable Gallery, or finds a rapt individual face in a clustered and restless-looking shoot of the Judson Dance Theater troupe. It’s a way to catch someone smiling and laughing in natural social reaction, as against the smile solicited by the camera in a solo encounter. Hujar’s individual sitters smile little. Sontag, in the famous reclining portrait, manages a not exactly humorous curving of the lips; the reclining William Burroughs’s very faint smile is more likely produced by the weight of his head on his raised hand. But in the world of noncommercial performers that he was drawn more and more to depicting, a wild and dissident exuberance was there to be captured.

Two pages are given to the contacts for the celebrated photo of members of the Gay Liberation Front running down West 19th Street in 1970: they’re seen from far off, a rumor on the horizon, then they rush repeatedly toward the camera, coming to a standstill in a cheerful panting huddle just in front of us. The selected image became a poster—“Come Out!!”—“papered over downtown in the weeks leading up to Christopher Street Liberation Day, the first Pride Parade,” Durbin writes, though he makes a tiny mistake in transcribing the words below as “Join the brothers and sisters of the Gay Liberation Front” when it should be “the sisters and brothers.” In the photo it’s the lesbians, happy and determined and ineffably more worldly-wise, who make up the surging front row, their arms around one another, the one on the left of the line reaching back to hook forward the nearest of the long-haired young men, several of whom are nearly hidden behind the women except for their raised fists. There are traces of self-consciousness in acting out their real defiance and joy on demand for the camera, “like practicing for a musical.” It’s nonetheless a moment of release and solidarity, and the challenges ahead seem suddenly surmountable. Yet as Martin Duberman noted of the photo in his book Stonewall twenty-three years later, “these ebullient troops seem to have no backup forces”; there are a mere sixteen people on this march, and the “tsunami wave” of heightened white light that hurtles them forward seems to isolate them too.

The Wonderful World That Almost Was tells its story forward rather than through the elegiac lens of the two artists’ premature deaths, yet this image of a joyful advance can’t help but foretoken the then-unimagined tsunami of AIDS. Since we cannot read ahistorically for long, Durbin’s narrative gains a heartbreaking power from our pervasive sense of the frailty and contingency of everything it charts.

entries.title: Boxcar to Nowhere
entries.summary: American lore about hoboes has sugared over the economic and environmental forces that drove people from their homes and onto the rails and roads in the first place, as a new history lays out.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
A hundred years ago, it seemed as if everyone wanted to be a hobo, at least if you were listening to the radio. Carl Sandburg’s 1927 American Songbag featured a whole section of hobo songs presenting the bum as a beau ideal. Children, most of whom would never see the inside of a boxcar, grew up singing “Hallelujah, I’m a Bum!,” recorded first by Harry McClintock in 1928 and repopularized by the New Christy Minstrels in the 1960s. Along with loads of other songs, it celebrated the paradoxical appeal of the rails and the open road: freedom allied with loneliness and destitution. John Lee Hooker’s “Hobo Blues,” Jimmie Rodgers’s “Hobo Bill’s Last Ride,” and Merle Haggard’s cover of Rodgers’s “Hobo’s Meditation” would become landmarks of the genre. The album cover of Haggard’s I’m a Lonesome Fugitive (1967) depicts him climbing aboard a freight car, a look of consummate fulfillment on his face.

Dreams of a tramp utopia, once termed “hobohemia,” produced classics of Americana.1 Recorded in the 1920s by McClintock, the rollicking hobo anthem “Big Rock Candy Mountain” envisions an itinerants’ paradise where cigarette trees bloom and streams of alcohol trickle down the rocks. It has since been recorded or performed by dozens of folk, pop, and country musicians, including Pete Seeger, Burl Ives, Bing Crosby, Tex Ritter, Johnny Cash, Roger Whittaker, the Highwaymen, and the Nashville string band Old Crow Medicine Show. Its sly salute to sin has become a hallmark of this particular form of counterculture: Wallace Stegner named a novel after the song, and it features prominently in the Coen brothers’ satirical adaptation of the Odyssey set in the American South, O Brother, Where Art Thou? (2000), itself an homage to an earlier hobo film, Preston Sturges’s 1941 Sullivan’s Travels.

The contradictory nature of the hobo, a character without home or possessions who embodied good-natured liberty and a gap-toothed joie de vivre, gave rise to a persistent sense of envy. As a result, Woody Guthrie’s fictionalized 1943 autobiography, Bound for Glory, exaggerated the extent of his riding the rails, and he would lean heavily on the bindle stiff gospel throughout his life and career, disappearing for weeks at a time after telling his wife he was going out for cigarettes. In one song he claimed, “I ain’t got no home in this world anymore”; in another he described the afterlife of a “Backdoor Bum”; in yet another he denounced “Old Man Trump,” the president’s father and Guthrie’s landlord in Brooklyn, for “racial hate.” His most famous song, “This Land Is Your Land,” remains an impassioned denunciation of private property and a hymn to the “freedom highway,” its pointed lyrics encouraging wanderers to flout the law:

As I went walking I saw a sign there,

And on the sign it said “No Trespassing.”

But on the other side it didn’t say nothing.

That side was made for you and me.

Shortly after arriving in New York City in 1961, Bob Dylan cast himself as Guthrie’s protégé, devouring Bound for Glory “cover to cover like a hurricane” and identifying so strongly with his mentor that he told a public relations flack at Columbia Records, his newly acquired label, that he’d made his way across country to the Big Apple in hobo fashion as if it were a career qualification. His 2004 memoir recalls the exchange:

“How did you get here?” he asked me.

“I rode a freight train.”

“You mean a passenger train?”

“No, a freight train.”

“You mean, like a boxcar?”

“Yeah, like a boxcar. Like a freight train.”

“Okay, a freight train.”

Dylan was a latter-day fabulist in the mold of Mark Twain, calling himself a “migrant worker” and claiming that he’d once worked for a circus. In fact he rode to New York in the backseat of an acquaintance’s ’57 Impala. Yet in his early days his impulse to establish street cred as a tramp was so intense that he told the folk singer Ramblin’ Jack Elliott, who suspected the younger singer of borrowing from Guthrie, that he had “learnt…songs from various hoboes he met on the road.” Elliott drily noted, “I didn’t argue about it.”

These colorful anecdotes, alongside the hobo songs Dylan began writing or performing (“I Am a Lonesome Hobo,” “Only a Hobo,” and “Freight Train Blues”), are reflections of the conflicted national character already present in Walt Whitman’s “Song of the Open Road”—“Afoot and light-hearted I take to the open road…the world before me”—and of course “Song of Myself,” our euphoric yawp to individualism, independence, self-reliance, and the worship of oceanic open spaces:

I tramp a perpetual journey (come listen all!)

signs are a rain-proof coat, good shoes, and a staff cut from the woods….

Not I, not any one else can travel that road for you

You must travel it for yourself.

As with the troubadours who followed, the Good Gray Poet hints that the rewards of the road and its journey to self-awareness may come at the cost of poverty and isolation.

High-spirited songs often cast hobo life as upbeat and fancy-free, but literary works on the theme were likely to involve grim accounts of penury and abuse: in Jack London’s 1907 memoir, The Road, a forerunner of Jack Kerouac, he describes getting picked up for vagrancy in Erie County, New York, and subsisting on bread and water while serving on a chain gang. John Steinbeck’s Of Mice and Men (1937) and The Grapes of Wrath (1939) were based in part on a series of articles he wrote in 1936 for The San Francisco News, “The Harvest Gypsies,” about the lives of migrant laborers who followed the harvest during the Great Depression. Capturing the dangers faced by these antiheroes as they dodged railroad police wielding billy clubs or ranch managers with guns, these accounts immersed the reader in the subjective sensory musk of the experience: the smoke of barrel fires, the pungent character of the slang, the desperate sweat of a Yankee Doodle strain of nostalgie de la boue.

What these distinctly American stories do not address, however, are the hard-to-discern economic and environmental forces that drove people from their homes and onto the rails and roads in the first place. Historians have long identified the aftermath of the Civil War as the origin, when homeless or wounded veterans looking for employment formed a “great army of tramps.” Some reach back further, interpreting colonial America as a “surplus” population from the old country, sent to the New World as a “solution to…the homelessness crisis of Tudor and Stuart England.”2

The Dust Bowl and the Great Depression have been seen as a major impetus behind the mass migrations of the 1930s, but less attention has been paid to the depression and the dust bowl of the 1890s and the wave of farm failures they produced, their boom-and-bust years signaling catastrophes to come. For that we have Robert Suits’s The Hobo: A History of America’s First Climate Migrants, a modern reassessment of the long road this country has traveled toward climate disaster and homelessness. In this punctilious work, we learn that hoboes were far from the simple stereotypes of the carefree, careworn, or hapless wanderers of song and story. They were, in fact, some of the hardest-working people out there.

According to Suits, the idea of the hobo (the etymology of the word is uncertain) emerged as soon as there were coal- or steam-powered engines. During boom years, migrant workers provided the muscle to serve the massive industrialized agriculture machine that settlers began busily erecting in the Midwest and the Great Plains as soon as they arrived on the scene. Manual labor was essential in what he calls our “climatically unstable hinterlands,” largely because early forms of mechanization, such as horse- or steam-powered threshing machines, left gaps in the system that could be filled only by human hands.

During good years, it was hoboes who were reaping, binding, winnowing, and threshing the American wheat crop. The low population density of the Dakotas, Kansas, and Oklahoma meant there were not enough farmers or resident laborers living in the Great Plains to perform necessary work. While some estimates put the number of homeless people in the early 1900s at half a million, from 1870 to 1930 there were between 100,000 and 200,000 itinerant workers—and this at a time when “migrant work, homelessness, and radicalism intertwined,” Suits writes. Around 1910, 100,000 were laboring in the intensive wheat-growing areas of Minnesota, the Dakotas, and Kansas while tens of thousands worked as lumbermen in the North Woods of Wisconsin and Minnesota. Thousands more worked in mines in Illinois, in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, and throughout the West. There were few in the South, where white supremacy held sway and labor was supplied mainly by sharecroppers. Hoboes were largely men, although 3 percent were women performing domestic labor, cooking and sewing for agricultural crews or in lumber camps. Small numbers of women also worked wheat harvests—a fact that male journalists found surprising.

Hoboes defined themselves as homeless, migratory, and seeking work. “Chasing the harvest,” they called it, looking to distinguish themselves from “tramps” or “bums” who eschewed labor and were perhaps stationary, hunkering down in towns or cities and presumably begging or stealing to get by. Communities and property owners paid little attention to such distinctions, even as employers desperate for migrant labor begged in newspaper advertisements for hands to bring in the crops or work coal seams.

The moment migrant laborers were no longer wanted, communities turned on them. Suits tells the illustrative story of the hoboes’ shifting fates in the Dakotas and the Northern Plains of the 1890s. The first year of the decade was relatively poor for wheat; 1891 was a record harvest. The following year promised to be even better, with grain fattening on reliable rains resulting from atmospheric lows and with little in the way of hail, floods, or damaging winds. In 1892 the bumper crop was so heavy that employers began panicking at the need for hands to haul it in.

Advertisement

Farmers greeted trains that year, offering “harvest hands” more than two dollars per day plus room and board (women were offered only two dollars a week to feed the men), and for the first time the railroads themselves reduced or waived fares on major trunk lines in an attempt to lure “teachers, businessmen, and even circuit court judges”—hoping to abet the transport of lucrative carloads of grain. That year there were barely enough workers to complete the harvest before it spoiled. Farmers and their hobo workforce produced 70 million bushels of wheat, “one for every citizen in the United States.”

The year 1893 was a different story. A drought year, it was a “nightmare,” Suits says, followed by year after year of drought, the worst period until the 1930s. At the same time, the price of wheat fell owing to a global wheat glut and an economic depression. Once-valued itinerant laborers were cast adrift, dismissed as lazy and shiftless and increasingly seen as a threat to towns and families. Where once “harvest hand” was an affectionate term for newborn babies, “tramps” were now denounced as dirty drunks. Newspapers reviled them in moral terms, hinting at fears that tramp life offered, in Suits’s words, “a haven for homosexuality and nonnormative behaviors” that would imperil women and children. The drought alone didn’t cause this violent shift in rhetoric, but the surplus of workers engendered by boom-and-bust eventually incited violence against homeless men. “The increasing suspicion of the harvest hand,” Suits argues, arose from “climatic conditions and the economic and penal systems around them.”

What emerges as a theme in The Hobo is the sheer nastiness of townsfolk, police, railroad bulls, and farmers themselves in dealing with the “tramp problem,” a viciousness baked into small-town attitudes since the Puritans gave shape to our national identity, with its moral superiority and hostility toward outsiders. “Police turfed hoboes from cars, criminals shot and beat them for their earnings, and on top of all that, farmers increasingly saw hoboes as employees and adversaries rather than friendly faces at the dinner table,” Suits writes. Even when they were working, they were suspected of loose morals and alcoholism.

In 1913 an editorial in The Mirror, a newspaper published by Minnesota’s Stillwater State Prison, described harvest hands who expected “a large drink of whiskey every morning,” two lunches carried to the field, and a “quart bottle of beer at dinner.” Not perhaps unreasonable for people doing hard labor in the fields from dawn to dusk—“killing work,” one called it—but the gracious meeting of these needs by a “Bohemian farmer” suggests how different self-righteous American pieties regarding alcohol and abstinence could be from somewhat more relaxed European attitudes. The writer noted that experienced hands returned to the same Bohemian settlement year after year: “The best harvest hands are hoboes, they do the work; but to keep them with you, they have to be treated according to their standard. The hobo’s idea of a good time is to have plenty of things to drink.”

The volatility of responses to harvest workers gave rise to a movement to unionize. In the 1910s Joe Hill, a so-called Wobbly, took up a popular vaudeville song, “Ta-Ra-Ra-Boom-De-Ay,” and recast the lyrics to promote the Industrial Workers of the World, which also adopted “Hallelujah, I’m a Bum!” as its anthem. In Hill’s version a worker drops his pitchfork, accidentally on purpose, into the cogs of the thresher machine, producing an unholy racket and a work shutdown: “Ta-ra-ra-boom-de-ay!/It made a noise that way.” It was an early version of what we would now call monkeywrenching.

Organizing strikes virtually every year, the IWW managed to raise harvest hand wages to four dollars per day in some parts of the Dakotas by 1917, but its actions became pitched battles between town vigilantes, ad hoc militias, and union organizers. Eventually the gains were threatened by increasing farm mechanization and a federal crackdown during World War I, when threats to the national food supply were characterized as antiwar and union “agitators” were swept up and arrested. Despite their obstreperousness and resistance to organization, hoboes were nonetheless involved in most of the major labor actions of their time. “The heart of our trouble today,” wrote one such radical, “lies in our having allowed private ownership in the big industries of the country.”

For many hoboes, wheat farming occupied summer and fall, lumbering the winter, but felling trees won them no respect either. Robert Frost’s early hobo poem in North of Boston (1914), “The Death of the Hired Man,” adopted the farmers’, not the laborers’, perspective, and his ambiguous response to vagrants is evident in a later work, “Two Tramps in Mud Time”:

Out of the woods two hulking tramps

(From sleeping God knows where last night,

But not long since in the lumber camps).

They thought all chopping was theirs of right.

Men of the woods and lumberjacks,

They judged me by their appropriate tool.

Except as a fellow handled an ax

They had no way of knowing a fool.

Arguably a bit hulking himself, Frost grudgingly acknowledges the tramps’ “need” as a “better right,” but he keeps on chopping, insisting that his purpose, “to unite/My avocation and my vocation,” is higher. The poet known for his dialogues chooses not to give them a voice.

Suits is at his sharpest when writing about the North Woods of Wisconsin, the legendary Big Woods that stretched across thousands of acres of the great Northland. He grew up among the scars concealed by a canopy of second growth,

wounds that have barely begun to heal…. You can see the past…in how nearly every tree is the same size; there were no old oaks or maples on my childhood street. Each of them, without exception, was not yet a century old.

Eloquent on the risks of felling massive trees and skidding logs down frozen rivers, he dissects an economy that relied on “raw” human kinetic energy to convert forests into lumber, with men functioning as metabolic engines, working shirtless in the freezing cold as they burned off enormous meals of five, six, or eight thousand calories a day. “A 1910 estimate of power use in the timber industry,” he says, “combined with what we know about camp food suggests humans probably supplied around a third of the total power,” itself perhaps an underestimate. Not surprisingly, Suits notes, hoboes often compared themselves to “draft animals,” lamenting the “horse work” they were required to perform.

Such labor was rewarded with disgusting living conditions: bunkhouses furnished with dirt floors, no ventilation, and verminous blankets. Men like those in Frost’s poem took to the roads searching for better conditions. P.K. Small, a lumberjack interviewed by a federal investigator, was missing half of his nose and had broken a hand, a leg, and a shoulder in various skidding accidents but said he dreaded the bunkhouses the most. Monotonous meals of salt pork or salt beef were filled out with bread or potatoes; drinking water was unsafe, with men sharing a common cup; typhoid fever, smallpox, and influenza were rampant. Accidents were greeted with shrugs. “A drowning did not even slow up the work,” according to a lumberjack in Wisconsin. “The drive had to go on.” Another man, ill with tuberculosis, said, “I got to keep on going till I drop. Every night I think I’m going to die.” Broken limbs and amputations were not uncommon, but there was no recourse for the maimed: private insurance policies excluded lumbering, along with mining and construction work. Such men generally ended up indigent, living in almshouses or begging for food.

The land was also broken: “The woodland that built most of the cities and towns of the Great Plains, from Chicago to tiny farmsteads in Montana, still has yet to regenerate fully, more than a century later.” Towns in the Northland with economies once dependent on lumber were left to shift to other forms of income or simply disappear.

Hoboes themselves began to vanish. Tractors and increasingly sophisticated forms of automation took their places on farms, and the North Woods were logged out by 1920. Lumberjacks moved on to lay waste to the Pacific Northwest and the pine forests of the South, and there, too, mechanization began replacing human labor. Successive union strikes helped to establish an eight-hour workday in northwestern lumber camps and mills, but by the 1950s the chainsaw took the place of axes and handsaws, and cars made commuting to lumber jobs possible for family men.

By the mid-twentieth century, the Great Plains were growing “wheat sick,” with yields depleted by years of monoculture. To meet the needs of farmers raising fruit in California and the sugar beets that were replacing wheat in the Midwest, families from Mexico were recruited in the border states, with some moving north to handle the beet crop. Asked by Congress why they were relying on immigrant labor, farmers admitted that Americans didn’t want to do manual labor anymore. Immigrants, meanwhile, found conditions as dirty, dangerous, and exploitative as the hoboes had and were likewise subjected to punitive violence, now embedded in the federal response of ICE.

There is no “clean end” to the history of hoboes, Suits says. Migrant manual laborers still fill what he calls “the interstices of the fossil economy,” the places where human hands are indispensable: they labor in slaughterhouses or in construction jobs or as pickers “in the vast warehouses of online retailers.” In fields, they tend and harvest apples, apricots, avocados, blueberries, carrots, cherries, chiles, grapes, lettuce, melons, mushrooms, raspberries, strawberries, and tomatoes. Yet these workers, “now racialized,” who fill grocery shelves are unceasingly devalued, with Republicans calling for “MASS DEPORTATION NOW!” at their national convention in 2024.

The capitalist system that produced and took advantage of hoboes is still visible today in the new hobo camps—tent cities under highway overpasses where the migrant poor, some 40 percent of whom are working (often two or three jobs), find temporary shelter. If today we were to ask, “O brother, where art thou?” the answer would be simple: a car in the Walmart parking lot. Even if you have a full-time job there, at the base pay of fourteen dollars an hour it would be impossible to afford housing or basic needs. Meanwhile, so-called right-to-work laws limiting union membership in twenty-six states have crippled organizations that might once have lobbied for higher pay and better conditions.

Suits acknowledges that the hoboes’ way of life was shaped by agricultural forces that no longer hold sway. But he points out that we nonetheless inherited from a previous century our heartless attitudes toward homeless and migratory workers and the rhetoric we use to revile them. The number of homeless people in the US, more than 745,000 as of 2025, is “roughly equal” to what it was then, even though the overall population has tripled. Yet the contempt for those who perform our killing work remains a testament to the nature of American generosity. There’s no hallelujah about it.

No one, it seems, envies the hobo or the homeless anymore. Dylan, our great troubadour of the open road, continues to lead a wandering life, restlessly touring year after year. He was scheduled to perform in Las Vegas in 2016 when the Nobel Committee announced that he’d won the prize for literature. He said nothing about the honor to his audience that night and did not respond to the committee for weeks. For an encore, though, he sang a Frank Sinatra song, perhaps an homage to his humblest idols:

I’m sentimental, so I walk in the rain

I’ve got some habits even I can’t explain

Could start for the corner, turn up in Spain

But why try to change me now?

entries.content:
My friend the bon vivant bookseller Michael Seidenberg of Brazenhead Books, which he ran out of his apartment in New York City, died in 2019. I’d known him since 1978, when as a teenager I apprenticed myself to his first shop. Michael loved pressing “lost” books and authors on me, and on anyone. A visit to one of his shops often concluded with taking home a novel one had not only not been seeking, but of which one had never heard. He would typically reduce the price of such a purchase, as a softening of the risk entailed in taking his word.

Michael was also an instinctive devil’s advocate. When I once spoke of my enthusiasm for trade paperback imprints dedicated specifically to reviving lost books, he surprised me. “Those are tombstones,” he told me (my quotation is a paraphrase from memory). “Being published by one of those presses that only publishes revivals, it’s the last heartbeat of a dying reputation. Presenting an author under the flag of rediscovery is the same thing as saying, ‘No one cared in the first place.’ After that, a book is officially dead forever.” He also pointed out how these imprints tended themselves to die out after just a handful of books.

With hindsight we can see what Michael missed in this particular contrarian flex. Not long before that conversation, Virago Books in the UK had launched the Virago Modern Classics. These displayed two strengths: the distinctive green spines that made one want to see whole shelves of them together, and a confidence, buoyed by their feminist imperatives, to keep rushing them out faster than one could read them, like a sea turtle laying a thousand eggs, knowing some will thrive but not knowing which ones. This created a map for success in future such enterprises, not that it could be guaranteed.1 Vintage Contemporaries followed in 1984, adopting the Virago strategies—attractive uniform editions, and a cornucopian blend of paperback originals and reissues that largely focused on living writers.

The next chapter in this story is best told by quoting the critic Elaine Blair. In a 2021 essay in these pages called “Averted Intimacies,” she speaks of the revival, spearheaded by the magazine A Public Space, of the nearly forgotten Bette Howland. This came, according to Blair,

amid a surge of interest in reissued titles. Cycles of obscurity and rediscovery may be a regular part of book publishing, but in recent years the number of reissues and—perhaps most significantly—the amount of review coverage they receive have been striking. In addition to the presses that specialize in reissues (NYRB Classics, the Feminist Press), other publishers have also revived out-of-print work (as Farrar, Straus and Giroux did with Lucia Berlin’s stories and New Directions with Fran Ross’s satirical novel Oreo).

I agree. We live in a continuing great era of rediscovered books. Starting in 1999, NYRB Classics doubled down on Virago’s and Vintage’s methods with its finer bindings and acid-free pages, creating a handfeel that made their series even more pleasing to read and collect, and by the quality of the curation and editing of the forewords, prefaces, introductions, translator’s notes, and afterwords surrounding each text. More recently, McNally Editions has met that standard, while other, somewhat less rapid-fire presses like Transit, Counterpoint, Pushkin, and Two Dollar Radio are also making terrific contributions.

Some presses will seem driven just to restore a given writer or two, like Steerforth did with Dawn Powell (triumphantly) and Isabel Bolton (less so). No doubt I’m missing some names. The libidinal energy of such rediscoveries parallels other “analog” revival booms, like that for vinyl records. Despite literature’s highbrow aura, the appetite for lost books echoes not only the world of used bookstores, but the present yearning for a less predigested, more incautious mode of cultural life that still lurks in living memory, or in our parents’ attics.

Not all the turtles’ eggs survive, either. If you believe in canons,2 then NYRB Classics may have boosted a few twentieth-century US contestants:3 John Williams’s Stoner (originally published 1965; reissued 2006) and Butcher’s Crossing (1960; 2007), Renata Adler’s Speedboat (1976; 2013), Don Carpenter’s Hard Rain Falling (1966; 2009), surely others.4 But this isn’t the Modern Library or Library of America, let alone Norton Critical Editions; the vibe is less proclamatory, more personal and intimate, the realm of a reader’s private pleasure. Perhaps you latched on to Lisa Tuttle’s My Death (2004; 2023), or Sasha Sokolov’s A School for Fools (1976; 2015). Me, I’m obsessed with Raymond Kennedy’s Ride a Cockhorse (1991; 2012) but can’t convince others that it’s a perfect allegory of the codependency of Trump’s inner circle, or really even get anyone to read it. And that’s OK. In this sense, Michael’s prophecy may be true: the present vogue for republication makes a nice last moment for some books destined to join the slew of forgotten others always receding behind us.

Advertisement

Michael, incidentally, became a great collector and purveyor of the Vintage Contemporaries and the NYRB Classics, which he loved both to read and to see lining up in delicious uniformity on his shelves. He was always lovably willing to contradict himself.

Wilfrid Sheed was born in London in 1930. The son of the Catholic publishers Frank Sheed and Maisie Ward, he grew up shuttling between England and the US. Though educated at Oxford before his aspirational leap to New York City and the beginning of his literary career, by his own account as a boy he’d fallen in love with baseball, not cricket or rugby, as well as with certain aspects of American popular culture like jazz and Broadway musicals. He survived childhood polio, the account of which finds its way into several of his fictions and his memoir of illness and recovery, In Love with Daylight (1995). His prodigious and versatile literary career encompassed nine works of fiction, three collections of critical essays, the memoir, and books on subjects as diverse as his fondnesses: baseball, jazz, Muhammad Ali, Clare Boothe Luce, and his parents. As a busy and prominent critic, he appears to have managed to walk a knife’s edge between fraternizing widely in Manhattan and on Key West, and being seen as a hit man in the Anatole Broyard, rip-the-jugular vein. Being a killer reviewer could be a bad fate socially, and also if one hoped to be critically embraced as a novelist. Which Sheed was. Though never drawing a wide readership, he was nominated for the National Book Award three times, and reviewed—says I, who’s been weighing the tangible results against the critical record—(spoiler alert) generously.

The key to that knife’s-edge walk and to the admiration and fellowship Sheed enjoyed among his contemporaries is likely the same: his tone, always urbane, ironic, lucid, and at times truly funny. This pertains especially when he’s strongly on-target (concerning, typically, great white males like Mailer, Waugh, Hemingway, Vidal); less so when he’s badly off (ahem, James Baldwin, ahem, feminism). Though Sheed regularly self-inoculates by dubbing himself a minor novelist, he enters readily into imaginative sympathy with these monsters of ambition, leaving intact their implicit importance at the center of our literary culture, no matter that the book or books at hand—sometimes several decades’ worth—have been declared inadequate.

On Hemingway, in these pages: “Fame settled in to stay and clamped his style into place, where it grew warped and gnarled like a tree in a cave.” Mailer:

It is no accident that Mailer wrote the first big war novel, subsequently managed to hook himself onto both the Beat Generation and the French Existentialists, jumped off in time to catch the Negro express, elbowed briefly to the front of the Peace Movement, worked Vietnam into a novel title (an almost infallible sign of charlatanry)…. And who is the first writer to tell us about the moon?

Sheed’s sentences are fizzy with asides, nudges, and flattery to the informed reader. They remind me of the Raymond Chandler one encounters in Chandler’s letters—another writer who cross-pollinated the archness and delicacy of an English education with a thrilled appetite for the funk of US vernacular. And both Chandler and Sheed seem to use that wit to manage a scathing disenchantment, though Sheed disguises his better than does Chandler.

Sheed died in 2011, and in 2024 McNally Editions republished his best novel, Office Politics (1966), with a foreword by Gerald Howard, to another round of mostly warm reviews; Electric Literature, following the author’s lead in self-depreciation, called it a “minor masterpiece.”

The novel depicts the eerily banal daily life of an influential small weekly magazine called The Outsider, a publication that could be mistaken for any number of real models like Dissent, The Nation, or even a teensy-tiny New Yorker. (Sheed, who was a critic and editor at Commonweal for several years, claims in an author’s note that The Outsider “resembles no magazine living or dead.”) The editor presiding over this “broken-down opinion machine” is an English expatriate named Gilbert Twining, who soaks up all available oxygen for miles around. His invitations to lunch are a form of alcoholic passive aggression. Nevertheless, the standard Twining establishes and the order he keeps are irreplaceable. When he goes on leave after a heart attack it sets in motion a low-key succession crisis among the staff: imagine Game of Thrones populated by versions of Bartleby the Scrivener. The small-stakes office comedy is rendered with delirious precision as the characters assassinate one another’s pretenses with the blunt instruments of the arched eyebrow and the declined copyedit. They might as well be attacking each other with empty staplers:

Advertisement

“Brian, where did you find this—this thing?”

“What thing?”

“This gold thing.”

“You mean Culpeper’s article on the gold standard? You know who Culpeper is, don’t you?”

“He’s no writer that I know.”

“Look, we’re lucky to have him, he’s one of Canada’s leading economists.”

“A commentary, a sad commentary.”

“I’ve been trying to get something out of him for years.”

“You’ve been wasting your time, is all I can say.”

By default, at least at first, we root for George Wren, a younger, half-endearing American editor with an actual home life and a bunch of secret poems stashed in his desk. Yet Sheed deploys Wren’s comparatively unspoiled viewpoint mainly to illustrate how little the younger man grasps about the balance of purely symbolic power and painfully nonsymbolic disappointment that Twining has devised to keep the magazine functioning even in his absence. The book seems ultimately designed to function as an expectations-humbling machine. No one here rates anything but the mildest sympathy, which is precisely what their creator has granted them, after cutting off their legs.

Still, the pleasures of Sheed’s wriggly sentences carry the day, earning the comparisons to Kingsley Amis and to Joshua Ferris’s Then We Came to the End (2007). Knowing I could score some first-edition Sheeds cheaply—I’d passed them by in used bookstores for years—I launched a further investigation into his fiction.

In fact, I went into a long Sheed-trance. This was an unforced error. My old zeal for deep dives—I once spent a year reading every book by Stanisław Lem—resulted in what an analyst calls transference. Because Sheed’s rueful demolitions recalled scoundrelish writers I’d grown up reading—e.g., J.P. Donleavy, Terry Southern, or early Joseph Heller—I was ready for him to reveal some iconoclastic force, to uncork his secret rage against the machine. Or else he might turn on himself and convert his deep injuries—the dislocations and illness of his childhood—into pain the reader took into his own body, as one does reading William Maxwell when he rehearses the early death of his mother.

Neither happened. Sheed does write about himself, in a kind of deflected or mock-puzzled way. His novels portray writers and editors, but critics especially: Max Jamison (1970) is about a poisonous theater critic; Transatlantic Blues (1978) depicts the hectic, vainglorious life of a celebrated cultural critic (half Mailer, half David Frost); and The Boys of Winter (1987) is narrated by a publisher turned novelist who is wrangling the work of several other novelists in an enclave in the Hamptons. These form a collective self-portrait of a middle-aged man so entombed in his younger self’s eagerness to rise within the status quo that all he can possibly do is generate endless cutting remarks from within it.

What’s barely glimpsed is the outside of life. The healthy alienation from received institutional structures that might have resulted from Sheed’s parents—who were famous for their fervent Catholicism but also clearly somewhat embarrassing to their son—or from his involuntarily international childhood and his polio years is shrugged away in favor of burrowing into cranky conformity, despite his mock protests. And he only allows us to infer his rejection of Catholic belief. Hearing his mother in a debate on the radio, he identifies with her interlocutor: “Here was a bright, possibly even sane woman showing him a world as bizarre as Dante’s.” Listening to his father’s eulogy at St. Patrick’s Cathedral, he says, “That day, at least, I believed every word of it.”

Sheed may have never met a difference he didn’t wish to split. In creating fictional self-surrogates bursting with rude intolerance, he appears to be running a compensatory game, one meant to smuggle in opinions that might get him disinvited from certain parties. This maneuver recalls the worst of Saul Bellow, though in Sheed’s hands it is fleeter and funnier. As in a book like Mr. Sammler’s Planet (1970) the unspoken script might read, “If you think I (the author behind the curtain) am a reactionary, just look at how bad things could get if I took the gloves off.” Politics aside, Sheed’s fiction too much takes its lead from his criticism. His narrative voice and his characters display a bottomless obsession with triangulation, mimicry, counterfeiting, imposture.

This passion for exposing fakery serves Sheed best in the only other fiction of his I can really recommend, The Blacking Factory (1968), a coming-of-age novella. Here, a boy named Jim Bannister, whirled between England and the US, tabulates the growth of his prosecutorial sensibility as he considers his father’s new girlfriend, and his father, and himself:

Lorraine talked in a Seven Sisters drawl that sounded suspect to Jim (although he knew this accent sounded fake even when it was done right), and this brought out a trace of latent North Boston in Mr. Bannister’s answers. It was like being able to look into people’s skin through a microscope. “Can’t you hear that she’s a phony?” he wanted to tell his father at one point, and then: “Can’t you hear that he’s a phony?” to Lorraine. Can’t you hear that we’re all phonies? When Jimmy chimed in himself, his own voice sounded just as silly as theirs, and the thought of having to listen to the three of them all summer became really quite depressing.

Even in this, Sheed’s punch is pulled with “really quite depressing”—as though the razor insight of Robert Musil had retreated into the stifled yawn of P.G. Wodehouse. Total skepticism isn’t necessarily a novelist’s enemy, but it finds a poor companion in consolation-seeking. Sheed’s skepticism is his fiddler crab’s gigantic claw; meanwhile his tiny claw, where he stores his sense of pain and loss, he can barely cinch open. Amazingly, this is even true in memoirs devoted to his parents and to his recovery from illness and addiction.

Something is being hidden, and though I’m no expert on Catholicism I think it may be Sheed’s reluctance to explain his retreat from belief. Perhaps he was too obedient to his legacy: the most Catholic of all great Catholic writers, G.K. Chesterton, was Sheed’s godfather. Instead, an unspecific God-that-failed haunts Sheed; each time he tries and fails to substitute Babe Ruth, jazz, or literature in that seat of authority he reenacts this primal disappointment. His prose, on the surface, is worthy of Chesterton’s, every sentence issued with a twist, every face peeled to show a new face underneath, a delight in paradox as a lens on all creation. Yet Chesterton’s paradoxes conceal—until they can’t—real belief, and a desire to persuade the reader of the existence of an absolute higher good. Sheed’s hint instead at a trauma or nostalgia that they simultaneously deny.

As Elaine Blair so mercilessly points out, there is a zero-sum effect at work when any book is published, or republished. The reading oxygen breathing in and out of individual brains to form the ecosphere supporting new writing—or other rediscoveries—is not limitless. Let me be merciless in turn: I don’t think we need more Sheed.
